q_0304.stem: A patient asks at what point the placenta is structurally complete. Which response is accurate?
options: The structure of the placenta is complete by the 12th week; it then grows wider until 20 weeks and afterward grows thicker
The structure is complete by 20 weeks, when it covers approximately half the uterine surface
The structure is complete by day 17, when the maternal-placental-embryonic circulation is established
The structure is not complete until 28 weeks, when placental hormone production peaks
q_0304.rationale: "The structure of the placenta is complete by the 12th week." The placenta "continues to grow wider until 20 weeks, when it covers approximately half of the uterine surface. It then continues to grow thicker" (p. 239).
q_0304.trap: (B) is the fact bank's named error — a stem asking when the placenta is fully formed wants 12 weeks, not 20. The 20-week milestone is about surface area, and the two milestones are easy to merge because they sit in consecutive sentences.

q_0305.stem: A nurse is reviewing early placental development. By which day is the maternal-placental-embryonic circulation in place, and what else happens then?
options: By day 17, when the embryonic heart starts beating
By day 7, at the moment of implantation
By day 28, when the neural tube closes
By the end of the eighth week, when the embryonic period ends
q_0305.rationale: "The maternal-placental-embryonic circulation is in place by day 17, when the embryonic heart starts beating" (p. 239). By the end of the third week, embryonic blood is circulating between the embryo and the chorionic villi.
q_0305.trap: (B) is the reflex pick because the placenta does begin to form at implantation, so implantation feels like the moment circulation begins. Formation starts there; a working circulation takes another ten days, and the two events are separated deliberately in the text.

q_0306.stem: A nursing student is asked to describe the cotyledons of the placenta. Which description is accurate?
options: There are 15 to 20 cotyledons, and each one is a functional unit
There are 15 to 20 cotyledons, which together make up one functional unit
There are approximately 200 cotyledons, each containing a single chorionic villus
Cotyledons are the maternal blood spaces between the villi
q_0306.rationale: "A third layer develops into anchoring septa, dividing the projecting decidua into separate areas called cotyledons. In each of the 15 to 20 cotyledons, the chorionic villi branch out, and a complex system of fetal blood vessels forms. Each cotyledon is a functional unit" (p. 239).
q_0306.trap: (B) keeps the right count and destroys the point, which is that the placenta is built of many independent functional units rather than one. (D) names the intervillous spaces, which are where exchange happens but are not the same structure.

q_0307.stem: A nurse is explaining why placental exchange becomes more efficient as pregnancy advances. Which explanation is accurate?
options: Permeability increases as the cytotrophoblast thins and disappears, leaving only the syncytium, the functional layer, by the fifth month
Permeability increases because additional cell layers are added to the villous membrane over time
Permeability is constant throughout pregnancy; only placental surface area changes
Permeability increases because maternal blood pressure rises through pregnancy
q_0307.rationale: Early exchange "is minimal at this time because the two cell layers of the villous membrane are too thick. Permeability increases as the cytotrophoblast thins and disappears." "By the fifth month, only the single layer of syncytium is left between the maternal blood and the fetal capillaries. The syncytium is the functional layer of the placenta" (p. 239).
q_0307.trap: (B) inverts the mechanism in the intuitive direction, since more tissue sounds like more capacity. The membrane gets thinner, not thicker, and the same syncytium is where the four placental hormones are produced.

q_0308.stem: A patient's home pregnancy test is positive 10 days after ovulation. Which hormone did the test detect, and what is its primary function in early pregnancy?
options: Human chorionic gonadotropin, which preserves the function of the ovarian corpus luteum
Human placental lactogen, which stimulates maternal metabolism to supply fetal nutrients
Estriol, which reflects placental functioning
Progesterone, which maintains the endometrium
q_0308.rationale: Human chorionic gonadotropin "can be detected in the maternal serum or urine by 8 to 10 days after ovulation, shortly after implantation. This hormone is the basis for pregnancy tests," and it "preserves the function of the ovarian corpus luteum, ensuring the continued supply of estrogen and progesterone needed to maintain the pregnancy" (p. 239). Its maximum level occurs at 60 to 70 days.
q_0308.trap: (D) names a hormone with a real early-pregnancy role, but progesterone is not what a pregnancy test measures. The chain runs one step further back: the test detects the hormone that keeps the corpus luteum making progesterone.

q_0309.stem: A patient at 26 weeks has a positive glucose screen. Which placental hormone increases resistance to insulin and is implicated in this finding?
options: Human placental lactogen, which is similar to a growth hormone and facilitates glucose transport across the placental membrane
Human chorionic gonadotropin, which peaks at 60 to 70 days and then declines
Estriol, the major estrogen secreted by the placenta
Progesterone, which decreases the contractility of the uterus
q_0309.rationale: Human placental lactogen, also known as human chorionic somatomammotropin, "is similar to a growth hormone" and "stimulates the maternal metabolism to supply nutrients needed for fetal growth." It "increases the resistance to insulin, facilitates glucose transport across the placental membrane, and stimulates breast development to prepare for lactation" (p. 239).
q_0309.trap: (B) is the mirror error of the previous item — the two protein hormones are easily swapped because both are placental and both are abbreviated from long names. The insulin-resistance clause is the discriminator, and it is what gestational diabetes stems are built on.

q_0310.stem: A nurse is explaining why the uterus stays quiet through most of pregnancy and then does not. Which pair of statements is accurate?
options: Progesterone decreases the contractility of the uterus, and estrogen stimulates myometrial contractility
Progesterone stimulates myometrial contractility, and estrogen decreases it
Both hormones decrease contractility, and labor begins when both fall to zero
Neither hormone affects contractility; labor onset is entirely mechanical
q_0310.rationale: Progesterone "maintains the endometrium, decreases the contractility of the uterus, and stimulates maternal metabolism and development of breast alveoli," while estrogen "stimulates uterine growth and uteroplacental blood flow" and "stimulates myometrial contractility" (pp. 239–240). One stated theory of labor onset is "the decline in the ratio of circulating levels of progesterone to the increased levels of estrogen."
q_0310.trap: (C) overstates the theory in the way the fact bank flags: the book describes a shift in the ratio between the two hormones, not an absolute fall of progesterone to zero. Placental estrogen production increases greatly toward the end of pregnancy, so the ratio can shift while progesterone remains high.

q_0311.stem: A provider orders a maternal estriol level to evaluate placental function. Why is estriol the appropriate measure rather than estradiol?
options: The major estrogen secreted by the placenta is estriol, whereas the ovaries produce mostly estradiol
The major estrogen secreted by the placenta is estradiol, and estriol is a metabolite of it
Estriol is produced by the corpus luteum and therefore reflects early pregnancy maintenance
Estriol is the only estrogen that crosses the placental membrane
q_0311.rationale: "The major estrogen secreted by the placenta is estriol, whereas the ovaries produce mostly estradiol. Estriol levels may be measured to determine placental functioning" (pp. 239–240). By 7 weeks the placenta is producing most of the maternal estrogens.
q_0311.trap: (B) swaps the two estrogens between their two sources, which is the whole basis of the test. If the ovaries were the placental estrogen's source, the level would say nothing about how the placenta is working.

q_0312.stem: A patient at 7 weeks of gestation has a luteal phase defect and asks why this matters now rather than later. Which explanation is accurate?
options: By around 9 weeks the corpus luteum regresses as the placenta takes over; miscarriage occurs if the corpus luteum stops functioning before the placenta produces sufficient estrogen and progesterone
The corpus luteum supports the pregnancy until term, so the risk continues throughout
The placenta produces sufficient progesterone from implantation onward, so corpus luteum function is never critical
The corpus luteum regresses at 20 weeks, when the placenta reaches its full width
q_0312.rationale: Progesterone comes from the corpus luteum early, and the placenta becomes the primary source; "by around 9 weeks, the corpus luteum regresses." "Miscarriage occurs if the corpus luteum stops functioning before the placenta is producing sufficient estrogen and progesterone" (pp. 239–240).
q_0312.trap: (B) is the reflex pick for anyone who knows the corpus luteum matters but not that there is a handoff with a date. Because there is a handoff, a luteal defect is an early-pregnancy risk specifically, and the window closes rather than persisting.

q_0313.stem: A patient asks how her antibodies reach her baby before birth. Which transfer mechanism carries maternal immunoglobulins across the placental membrane?
options: Pinocytosis, which transfers large molecules such as albumin and gamma globulins
Active transport against the concentration gradient
Simple diffusion, as with water and small electrolytes
Facilitated diffusion, as with glucose
q_0313.rationale: Pinocytosis is "a mechanism used for transferring large molecules such as albumin and gamma globulins across the placental membrane," and it "conveys the maternal immunoglobulins that provide early passive immunity to the fetus" (p. 240).
q_0313.trap: (B) is the reflex pick because active transport sounds like the mechanism that would handle something as important as immunity. Size is what decides here, not importance: the immunoglobulins are too large for the diffusion and carrier mechanisms, so the membrane engulfs them.

q_0314.stem: A nurse is sorting substances by how they cross the placenta. Select all the statements that are accurate.
options: Water and most electrolytes with a molecular weight less than 500 cross by simple diffusion
Glucose is transported from mother to fetus by facilitated diffusion
Amino acids and calcium are transported against the concentration gradient by active transport
The majority of medications cross by passive diffusion
Oxygen is actively extracted from maternal blood by the placenta
q_0314.rationale: "Water and most electrolytes with a molecular weight less than 500 readily diffuse through the membrane." "Fetal demand for glucose is high, and it is transported from mother to fetus by facilitated diffusion." "Amino acids and calcium are transported against the concentration gradient." "The majority of medications cross the placenta through passive diffusion" (p. 240).
q_0314.trap: (E) is the single wrong option, and it is the error the fact bank flags in the oxygenation section: the placenta moves gases by diffusion, not by active extraction. It is attractive because the fetus does obtain oxygen efficiently, but the efficiency comes from fetal adaptations rather than from placental work.

q_0315.stem: A patient with diabetes asks why her baby's blood sugar would be lower than hers if glucose crosses freely. Which explanation is accurate?
options: The fetal concentration of glucose is lower because of rapid metabolism of glucose by the fetus
The fetal concentration is lower because the placenta consumes most of the glucose it transports
The fetal concentration is lower because glucose crosses only by active transport against a gradient
The fetal concentration is normally higher than maternal, so the premise is incorrect
q_0315.rationale: "The fetal concentration of glucose is lower than the glucose level in the maternal blood because of rapid metabolism of glucose by the fetus" (p. 240). Glucose crosses by facilitated diffusion, which follows the gradient rather than opposing it.
q_0315.trap: (B) attributes the gradient to the placenta rather than to the fetus, which is the error the fact bank names. The distinction matters for the diabetes cascade: because the gradient is driven by fetal consumption, maternal hyperglycemia raises fetal glucose directly and drives fetal hyperinsulinemia.

q_0316.stem: A nursing student is asked to name the metabolic functions of the placenta. Which set is correct?
options: Respiration, nutrition, excretion, and storage
Respiration, circulation, filtration, and immunity
Nutrition, excretion, thermoregulation, and hematopoiesis
Respiration and nutrition only; the fetal kidneys handle excretion
q_0316.rationale: "The metabolic functions of the placenta are respiration, nutrition, excretion, and storage." Oxygen and carbon dioxide diffuse in opposite directions, so "the placenta functions as lungs for the fetus"; carbohydrates, proteins, calcium, and iron are stored in the placenta; and fetal metabolic wastes cross into maternal blood "for excretion by the maternal kidneys" (p. 240).
q_0316.trap: (D) is the substantive error rather than a list error, and it inverts the chapter's central point. The fetus does not need functioning kidneys in utero precisely because the placenta acts as the organ of excretion, which is why renal failure declares itself at birth rather than before it.

q_0317.topic: fetal circulation and the three shunts
q_0317.stem: Which fetal shunt allows blood to bypass the liver, and where does it carry blood?
options: The ductus venosus, which carries blood from the umbilical vein into the inferior vena cava
The ductus arteriosus, which carries blood from the pulmonary artery into the aorta
The foramen ovale, which carries blood from the right atrium into the left atrium
The ductus venosus, which carries blood from the pulmonary artery into the aorta
q_0317.rationale: At the liver the umbilical vein "divides into two branches; one branch circulates some oxygenated blood through the liver. Most of the blood passes through the ductus venosus into the inferior vena cava" (p. 245). Of the three shunts, only the ductus venosus bypasses the liver.
q_0317.trap: (D) keeps the correct shunt name and attaches the ductus arteriosus's route to it, which is the harder error because naming the shunt feels like answering the question. Both ducts share a word, and only one of them has anything to do with the liver.

q_0318.topic: fetal circulation and the three shunts
q_0318.stem: A newborn's ductus arteriosus fails to close. Which connection has remained open, and what did it bypass in fetal life?
options: The pulmonary artery to the aorta, bypassing the lungs
The right atrium to the left atrium, bypassing the lungs
The umbilical vein to the inferior vena cava, bypassing the liver
The aorta to the pulmonary vein, bypassing the left ventricle
q_0318.rationale: The ductus arteriosus runs from the pulmonary artery to the aorta, "distal to the point of exit of the arteries supplying the head and arms." Because the fetal lungs do not function for gas exchange, "a special circulatory pathway, the ductus arteriosus, bypasses the lungs" (p. 245). A small amount of blood circulates through the resistant lung tissue, but the majority follows the lower-resistance path through the duct.
q_0318.trap: (B) describes the foramen ovale, and it is attractive because both structures bypass the lungs. The fact bank's discrimination is worth holding exactly: two shunts bypass the lungs and only one bypasses the liver, so "bypasses the lungs" cannot by itself identify a shunt.

q_0319.topic: fetal circulation and the three shunts
q_0319.stem: A nurse is teaching about the three fetal shunts. Select all the statements that are accurate.
options: The ductus venosus bypasses the liver
The foramen ovale carries blood from the right atrium to the left atrium
The ductus arteriosus carries blood from the pulmonary artery to the aorta
Both the foramen ovale and the ductus arteriosus allow blood to bypass the lungs
The ductus venosus bypasses the lungs
q_0319.rationale: The figure caption states that "three shunts permit most of the blood to bypass the liver and lungs: (1) ductus venosus, (2) foramen ovale, and (3) ductus arteriosus" (p. 245). The ductus venosus runs from the umbilical vein to the inferior vena cava, bypassing the liver; the foramen ovale opens from the right atrium into the left atrium; and the ductus arteriosus runs from the pulmonary artery to the aorta.
q_0319.trap: (E) is the single wrong option, and it is the one the fact bank predicts will be checked — an item naming all three shunts plus "ductus venosus bypasses the lungs" is testing precisely this. The word "ductus" appears in two shunt names, which is what makes their destinations easy to trade.

q_0320.topic: fetal circulation and the three shunts
q_0320.stem: Why does fetal circulation deliver the most oxygen-rich blood to the heart, head, neck, and arms rather than distributing it evenly?
options: This pattern enhances cephalocaudal, or head-to-rump, development of the fetus
The lower body has no arterial supply until after birth
The liver requires the least oxygen and is therefore supplied last
The pattern is incidental and has no stated developmental purpose
q_0320.rationale: Blood passing through the foramen ovale into the left ventricle is squeezed into the aorta, "where the arteries supplying the heart, head, neck, and arms receive most of the oxygen-rich blood." "This pattern of supplying the highest levels of oxygen and nutrients to the head, neck, and arms enhances the cephalocaudal (head-to-rump) development of the embryo/fetus" (p. 245).
q_0320.trap: (D) is the pick for a learner who has memorized the route without the reason, and the reason is what makes later material cohere — head-sparing in fetal growth restriction is the same principle under stress.

q_0321.topic: fetal circulation and the three shunts
q_0321.stem: Deoxygenated blood returning from the fetal head and arms enters the right atrium through the superior vena cava. Where does the majority of it go next?
options: Into the right ventricle, out the pulmonary artery, and through the ductus arteriosus into the aorta
Through the foramen ovale into the left atrium and out the aorta
Into the pulmonary circulation, where it is oxygenated by the fetal lungs
Directly into the umbilical vein for return to the placenta
q_0321.rationale: "Deoxygenated blood returning from the head and arms enters the right atrium through the superior vena cava. This blood is directed downward into the right ventricle, where it is squeezed into the pulmonary artery." "A small amount of blood circulates through the resistant lung tissue, but the majority follows the path with less resistance through the ductus arteriosus into the aorta" (p. 245).
q_0321.trap: (B) applies the foramen ovale's route to the wrong stream. Blood arriving from the inferior vena cava crosses the foramen ovale; blood arriving from the superior vena cava is directed to the right ventricle instead, and keeping the two streams separate is what the fetal heart is arranged to do. (D) reverses the umbilical vein's direction.

q_0322.stem: A nurse is explaining how the fetus obtains enough oxygen across a placenta rather than through lungs. Select all the special characteristics the chapter names.
options: Fetal hemoglobin has a high affinity for oxygen and carries 20% to 30% more oxygen than maternal hemoglobin
The hemoglobin concentration of the fetus is approximately 50% greater than that of the mother
The fetal heart rate of 110 to 160 beats per minute gives a cardiac output per unit of body weight higher than an adult's
The fetus has a larger lung surface area relative to body weight than an adult
q_0322.rationale: "The following three special characteristics enable the fetus to obtain sufficient oxygen from the maternal blood": fetal hemoglobin's higher affinity and 20% to 30% greater carrying capacity, a hemoglobin concentration approximately 50% greater than the mother's, and a fetal heart rate of 110 to 160 beats per minute producing higher cardiac output per unit of body weight (p. 246).
q_0322.trap: (D) is the single wrong option and it is wrong in a revealing way: the fetal lungs are not participating in gas exchange at all, so no lung property can be one of the adaptations. The three real adaptations are all about the blood and the pump, which is the pattern worth holding.

q_0323.stem: Why is a fetal heart rate of 110 to 160 beats per minute an oxygenation advantage rather than simply a normal value?
options: It produces a cardiac output per unit of body weight that is higher than an adult's, moving more blood through the placenta per minute
It reflects immaturity of the fetal conduction system and confers no advantage
It compensates for the low oxygen affinity of fetal hemoglobin
It allows the fetal lungs to participate in gas exchange before birth
q_0323.rationale: The third named adaptation is that "the fetal heart rate is 110 to 160 beats/min, making the cardiac output per unit of body weight higher than that of an adult" (p. 246).
q_0323.trap: (C) inverts the first adaptation. Fetal hemoglobin has a high affinity for oxygen, not a low one, so a rationale built on compensating for poor affinity contradicts the item next to it in the same list.

q_0324.stem: A patient asks why her baby is not harmed by having oxygen delivered through the placenta instead of lungs. Which statement about fetal hemoglobin is accurate?
options: It has a high affinity for oxygen and carries 20% to 30% more oxygen than maternal hemoglobin
It has a lower affinity for oxygen than maternal hemoglobin, which allows easier release to the tissues
It carries the same amount of oxygen as maternal hemoglobin but is present in lower concentration
It is identical to adult hemoglobin and confers no advantage
q_0324.rationale: "Fetal hemoglobin has a high affinity for oxygen and carries 20% to 30% more oxygen than maternal hemoglobin," and "the hemoglobin concentration of the fetus is approximately 50% greater than that of the mother" (p. 246).
q_0324.trap: (B) is the plausible-sounding inversion, since a lower affinity genuinely would help unload oxygen at the tissues. The fetal problem is acquiring oxygen across a membrane from maternal blood, not releasing it, so the adaptation runs toward higher affinity. (C) reverses the concentration finding as well.

q_0325.stem: An amniocentesis at 35 weeks reports a lecithin/sphingomyelin ratio of 2:1. How should the nurse interpret this?
options: The fetal lungs are deemed mature, a value reached at approximately the middle of the third trimester
The fetal lungs are immature, since a ratio of at least 4:1 is required
The result is uninterpretable without a simultaneous phosphatidylglycerol level
The ratio reflects renal rather than pulmonary maturity
q_0325.rationale: "The measure of lecithin in relation to sphingomyelin is used to determine fetal lung maturity. When the L/S ratio reaches 2:1, the fetal lungs are deemed mature," which "occurs approximately in the middle of the third trimester" (p. 246).
q_0325.trap: (B) raises a correctly remembered threshold to a wrong number, which is the standard way this item is missed. The 1.2:1 value that also appears in this chapter is the 30-to-31-week figure, not a target.

q_0326.stem: A student asks why fetal lung maturity is expressed as a ratio rather than as a single surfactant level. Which explanation is accurate?
options: Lecithin is detectable at approximately 21 weeks and increases after week 24, whereas sphingomyelin remains constant, so the ratio tracks the rising component against a fixed reference
Sphingomyelin rises steadily while lecithin remains constant, so the ratio tracks sphingomyelin
Both phospholipids rise together, and the ratio corrects for amniotic fluid volume
The ratio corrects for maternal blood contamination of the specimen
q_0326.rationale: Lecithin is "the most critical alveolar surfactant required for postnatal lung expansion. It is detectable at approximately 21 weeks and increases in amount after week 24," while sphingomyelin "remains constant in amount" (p. 246).
q_0326.trap: (B) swaps which phospholipid is the variable one, and the fact bank names this as the test of whether the ratio is understood or merely memorized. If the denominator were the rising value, the ratio would move the wrong way as the lungs matured.

q_0327.stem: Besides the lecithin/sphingomyelin ratio, which findings indicate fetal lung maturity?
options: Phosphatidylglycerol, detectable at about 36 weeks, indicating very low risk for respiratory distress syndrome, and a lamellar body count above 50,000
Phosphatidylglycerol detectable at about 24 weeks, and a lamellar body count below 50,000
An absent phosphatidylglycerol level with a rising sphingomyelin level
The presence of meconium in the amniotic fluid
q_0327.rationale: Phosphatidylglycerol is detectable "at about 36 weeks," and "its presence indicates very low risk for respiratory distress syndrome." A lamellar body count above 50,000 "indicates lung maturity"; lamellar bodies are "surfactant-containing particles within the alveoli" (p. 246).
q_0327.trap: (B) inverts the lamellar body threshold, turning a floor into a ceiling. (D) is a real amniotic fluid finding attached to the wrong question — meconium in the fluid points to breech presentation or fetal hypoxia, not to lung maturity.

q_0328.stem: A patient with gestational diabetes at 37 weeks has an estimated fetal weight above the 90th percentile. What should the nurse anticipate about this fetus's lungs?
options: They may be immature despite the large size, because hyperinsulinemia blocks lung maturation
They are certainly mature, because lung maturity tracks fetal size
They are accelerated in maturity, because maternal diabetes stresses the fetus
Lung maturity cannot be affected by maternal metabolic conditions
q_0328.rationale: "Gestational diabetes and chronic glomerulonephritis can inhibit fetal lung maturity" (p. 246). In fetuses of mothers with uncontrolled diabetes, maternal hyperglycemia produces fetal hyperglycemia, "stimulating hyperinsulinemia and islet cell hyperplasia. This results in a macrosomic (large) fetus. Hyperinsulinemia also blocks lung maturation, placing the neonate at risk for respiratory distress and hypoglycemia when the maternal glucose source is lost at birth" (p. 247).
q_0328.trap: (B) is the trap the fact bank names outright — assuming a macrosomic infant must have mature lungs. Size and maturity are driven by the same hormone in opposite directions here, so the infant can be large and immature at once. (C) applies the acceleration rule, which belongs to maternal hypertension, placental dysfunction, infection, and corticosteroid use, not to diabetes.

q_0329.stem: A neonate born by scheduled cesarean at 38 weeks without labor develops tachypnea and has crackles. Which explanation does the chapter give?
options: Neonates born by scheduled cesarean before 39 weeks without labor have an increased risk of transient tachypnea of the newborn, with crackles for the first 24 to 48 hours
The absence of thoracic compression during vaginal birth is now understood to be the sole cause of retained lung fluid
Lung fluid is produced only after birth, so early cesarean birth cannot affect it
Crackles at this age indicate pneumonia until proven otherwise
q_0329.rationale: "Neonates born by scheduled cesarean birth before 39 weeks' gestation without labor have an increased risk of transient tachypnea of the newborn and are likely to have crackles in their lungs for the first 24 to 48 hours." Lung fluid clearance "was originally attributed to the thoracic compression during vaginal birth; current thinking is that ... it begins well in advance of term birth" (p. 246).
q_0329.trap: (B) states the older explanation as though it were current, and the fact bank flags exactly this: do not attribute clearance solely to the thoracic squeeze. The distinction matters because clearance beginning well before birth is what makes gestational age, not mode of birth alone, the operative variable.

q_0330.stem: A nursing student is asked where blood formation first occurs in the developing human and how the site changes. Which sequence is correct?
options: Yolk sac in the third week, fetal liver from the sixth week, then bone marrow, spleen, thymus, and lymph nodes seeded in weeks 8 to 11
Fetal liver in the third week, then yolk sac, then bone marrow
Bone marrow from the third week onward, with no earlier site
Placenta in the third week, then fetal liver from the sixth week
q_0330.rationale: Hematopoiesis, "the formation of blood, occurs in the yolk sac ... beginning in the third week." Hematopoietic stem cells seed the fetal liver in the fifth week and hematopoiesis begins there in the sixth, which "accounts for the relatively large size of the liver between the seventh and ninth weeks." Stem cells seed the bone marrow, spleen, thymus, and lymph nodes in weeks 8 to 11 (p. 246).
q_0330.trap: (C) is the reflex pick from adult physiology, where marrow is the only answer. The sequence matters clinically because it explains the disproportionately large fetal liver at 7 to 9 weeks, which is otherwise a puzzling finding on early imaging.

q_0331.stem: An Rh-negative patient has a miscarriage at 8 weeks of gestation. Is she at risk for isoimmunization?
options: Yes; blood-type antigens are present on fetal erythrocytes soon after the sixth week, so she is at risk in any pregnancy lasting longer than 6 weeks after fertilization
No; isoimmunization can occur only after a term birth
No; fetal red cells do not carry antigens until the third trimester
Yes, but only if the pregnancy was ectopic rather than intrauterine
q_0331.rationale: "The antigenic factors that determine blood type are present in the erythrocytes soon after the sixth week. For this reason an Rh-negative woman is at risk for isoimmunization in any pregnancy that lasts longer than 6 weeks after fertilization" (p. 246).
q_0331.trap: (B) is the error the fact bank names, and it is the one with real consequences — confining the risk to term birth misses every early-loss scenario, including miscarriage, ectopic pregnancy, and induced abortion, all of which are prophylaxis indications.

q_0332.stem: A patient asks what "viability" means for her fetus. Which response reflects both definitions the chapter gives?
options: A standard statutory definition is 20 weeks of gestation with a birth weight of 350, 400, or 500 g and varies by state, while clinically infants at 22 to 25 weeks are on the threshold of viability
Viability is uniformly defined nationally as 24 weeks of gestation
Viability is defined solely by birth weight, without reference to gestational age
Viability begins at 28 weeks, when surfactant production is sufficient
q_0332.rationale: Viability is "the capability of the fetus to survive outside the uterus and is usually defined by fetal weight and pregnancy duration for statistical and legal purposes." "A standard definition is 20 weeks' gestation and birth weight of 350, 400, or 500 g, but this varies by state. Nurses must be aware of the laws in their states," while "infants who are 22 to 25 weeks of gestation are on the threshold of viability" (p. 241). The limits on survival are "CNS function and the oxygenation capability of the lungs."
q_0332.trap: (B) supplies the false comfort of a single national number, and the source says the opposite — the definition varies by state, which is why the chapter tells nurses to know their own state's law. The two definitions serve different purposes, and the stem decides which is being asked for.

q_0333.stem: A patient at 30 weeks is exposed to a substance known to be toxic. Which type of harm is most consistent with an exposure at this stage?
options: Functional damage to the central nervous system, since from 9 weeks the fetus is less vulnerable to teratogens except those affecting CNS function
Major structural malformation of the limbs and heart, since these organs are still forming
No harm is possible after the embryonic period ends
Immediate fetal demise, since the fetus has no remaining adaptive capacity
q_0333.rationale: "The stage of the fetus begins at 9 weeks," and during this period the fetus "is less vulnerable to teratogens except for those affecting functioning of the central nervous system" (p. 241). Stressors "cause damage to the CNS long after the vulnerable embryonic time for malformations in other organ systems," resulting in "cerebral palsy, neuromuscular impairment, intellectual disability, and learning disabilities" (p. 247).
q_0333.trap: (B) applies the embryonic-period rule to a fetal-period exposure. Structural malformations belong to weeks 3 through 8, when organs are forming; a third-trimester exposure item is a functional item, and mixing the two windows is what the distinction is there to prevent.

q_0334.stem: A nurse is teaching about fetal immunity. Select all the statements that are accurate.
options: Immunoglobulin G is the only immunoglobulin that crosses the placenta, providing passive acquired immunity to specific bacterial toxins
The fetus produces immunoglobulin M by the end of the first trimester
Immunoglobulin A is not produced by the fetus but is present in large amounts in colostrum
The normal-term neonate can fight infection, but not as effectively as an older child
All three immunoglobulin classes cross the placenta in the third trimester
q_0334.rationale: "The only immunoglobulin that crosses the placenta, immunoglobulin G (IgG), provides passive acquired immunity to specific bacterial toxins." The fetus "produces IgM by the end of the first trimester." "IgA is not produced by the fetus; however, colostrum, the precursor to breast milk, contains large amounts of IgA." "The normal-term neonate can fight infection but not so effectively as an older child. The preterm infant is at much greater risk for infection" (p. 248).
q_0334.trap: (E) is the single wrong option and it erases the distinction the whole section rests on. Because only immunoglobulin G crosses, an elevated immunoglobulin M level in cord blood cannot have come from the mother and therefore implies intrauterine infection — a deduction that is impossible if all three classes cross.

q_0335.stem: A patient at 20 weeks reports feeling fetal movement for the first time and asks whether this is expected. Which response reflects the chapter's developmental timetable?
options: Yes; fetal movements become strong enough for the mother to feel at about 20 weeks, and the fetus responds to sound by 24 weeks
No; maternal perception of movement is not expected until 28 weeks
Yes, but it indicates advanced gestational age, since movement is usually felt at 30 weeks
No; muscular movements cannot be detected by any method until 24 weeks
q_0335.rationale: Table 12.2 places "fetal movements strong enough for mother to feel" at 20 weeks, with muscular movements detectable by examination at 16 weeks, meconium in the bowel by 16 weeks, and hearing at 24 weeks (pp. 242–245). "Fetuses respond to sound by 24 weeks," and the fetus habituates to noises heard repeatedly (p. 247).
q_0335.trap: (D) conflates two different milestones from adjacent rows of the same table — movements can be detected at 16 weeks by examination, but maternal perception of them is a separate, later event. The table lists the two separately for exactly that reason.

q_0336.stem: A newborn receives prophylactic vitamin K. Which reasoning chain explains why?
options: The sterile fetal gut cannot synthesize vitamin K, so coagulation factors II, VII, IX, and X cannot be synthesized in the fetal liver, and the deficiency persists for several days after birth
The fetal liver is too immature to synthesize any coagulation factors until several weeks after birth
Vitamin K is destroyed by the placenta, so fetal stores are depleted at birth
Coagulation factors V and VIII cannot be synthesized because of maternal antibody transfer
q_0336.rationale: "Coagulation factors II, VII, IX, and X cannot be synthesized in the fetal liver because of the lack of vitamin K synthesis in the sterile fetal gut. This coagulation deficiency persists after birth for several days and is the rationale for the prophylactic administration of vitamin K to the newborn" (p. 247).
q_0336.trap: (D) names the wrong factors, and (B) attributes the deficiency to general hepatic immaturity rather than to the specific missing vitamin. The fact bank flags both: the chain has four checkable links, and a distractor that breaks any one of them is testing whether it was learned as a chain or as a conclusion.

q_0337.stem: A nurse is explaining why newborns, especially preterm ones, are prone to jaundice. Which explanation is accurate?
options: In fetal life unconjugated bilirubin is cleared by the placenta, so the glucuronyl transferase enzyme needed for conjugation is present in amounts less than those required after birth
The fetal liver conjugates bilirubin efficiently, but the newborn gut reabsorbs it
Bilirubin is produced only after birth, when fetal hemoglobin begins to break down
The placenta produces glucuronyl transferase, which the newborn must begin making at birth
q_0337.rationale: "During fetal life the liver does not have to conjugate bilirubin for excretion because the unconjugated bilirubin is cleared by the placenta. Therefore the glucuronyl transferase enzyme needed for conjugation is present in amounts less than those required after birth. This predisposes the neonate, especially the preterm infant, to hyperbilirubinemia" (p. 247).
q_0337.trap: (D) relocates the enzyme to the placenta, which sounds plausible because the placenta is doing the clearing. The enzyme is fetal and simply under-produced, since there has been no demand for it — an instance of the chapter's central pattern, in which a placental function becomes a newborn problem the moment the cord is cut.

q_0338.stem: A term newborn becomes hypothermic and has an increased work of breathing. Which hepatic store is the major source of energy under this stress, and how large is it?
options: Glycogen, which at term is stored at twice adult levels
Iron, which at term is stored at twice adult levels
Glycogen, which at term is stored at half adult levels
Brown fat, which is stored in the liver beginning at week 9
q_0338.rationale: The fetus stores glycogen in the liver beginning at week 9 or 10, and "at term, glycogen stores are twice those of an adult. Glycogen is the major source of energy for the fetus and neonate stressed by intrauterine hypoxia, extrauterine loss of the maternal glucose supply, the work of breathing, or cold" (p. 247).
q_0338.trap: (D) names a real store laid down for exactly this purpose, but brown fat is deposited between 26 and 30 weeks in preparation for extrauterine cold stress and is not a hepatic glycogen store. The chapter names glycogen specifically as the energy source under these four stressors, and cold is one of the four.

q_0339.stem: A parent asks when their exclusively breastfed infant might need supplemental iron. Which fact from the chapter is relevant?
options: If maternal intake was sufficient, the fetus stores enough iron to last 5 months after birth
Fetal iron stores are depleted within the first 2 weeks after birth
Iron cannot be stored by the fetus and must be supplied from birth
Fetal iron stores last approximately 2 years after birth
q_0339.rationale: "If the maternal intake is sufficient, the fetus can store enough iron to last 5 months after birth" (p. 247). Iron is also among the substances stored in the placenta for ready access to meet fetal needs.
q_0339.trap: (B) and (D) bracket the correct figure on both sides, which is how a half-remembered duration is caught. The clause that carries the clinical weight is the conditional one: the 5-month store assumes sufficient maternal intake, so maternal iron status during pregnancy determines when infant supplementation becomes necessary.

q_0340.stem: A nurse is explaining why fetal renal failure may not be apparent before birth. Which statement is accurate?
options: The placenta acts as the organ of excretion and maintains fetal water and electrolyte balance, so the fetus does not need functioning kidneys in utero, but the kidneys are required immediately at birth
The fetal kidneys are the primary organ of excretion from the end of the first trimester onward
Fetal renal failure always presents as hydramnios before birth
The newborn kidney concentrates urine as effectively as an adult kidney, so the transition is uneventful
q_0340.rationale: "Because the placenta acts as the organ of excretion and maintains fetal water and electrolyte balance, the fetus does not need functioning kidneys while in utero. However, at birth, the kidneys are required immediately for excretory and acid-base regulatory functions." At term "the GFR is low, and the kidneys lack the ability to concentrate urine," making the newborn "more susceptible to both overhydration and dehydration" (p. 247).
q_0340.trap: (C) inverts the amniotic fluid finding: absent or reduced fetal urine output produces oligohydramnios, not hydramnios, so renal failure that does declare itself before birth does so as too little fluid. (D) contradicts the stated limitation that makes newborn fluid management delicate.

q_0341.stem: A patient is told she is carrying dizygotic twins. Which statement about the membranes and placentas is always true?
options: There are always two amnions, two chorions, and two placentas that may be fused
There is always one chorion and one placenta shared by both fetuses
The membrane arrangement depends on when the zygote divided
There is always one amnion shared by both fetuses
q_0341.rationale: Dizygotic twins arise when multiple mature ova are "fertilized by separate sperm," and there "are always two amnions, two chorions, and two placentas that may be fused" (p. 248). They can be the same sex or different sexes and are genetically "no more alike than siblings born at different times."
q_0341.trap: (C) applies the monozygotic rule to the dizygotic case. Membrane arrangement is a timing question only when a single zygote divides; with two separate zygotes there was never a shared structure to divide, so the arrangement is fixed rather than variable.

q_0342.stem: A patient carrying monozygotic twins asks why some identical twins share a placenta and others do not. Which explanation is accurate?
options: The arrangement depends on when division occurs: soon after fertilization gives two amnions, two chorions, and two placentas, while division between 4 and 8 days, the most common timing, gives two amnions, one chorion, and one placenta
All monozygotic twins share one placenta and one chorion regardless of timing
The arrangement depends on the sex of the fetuses
Division after the eighth day gives two separate placentas with no shared membranes
q_0342.rationale: Division "soon after fertilization" produces "two embryos, two amnions, two chorions, and two placentas that can be fused"; division "between 4 and 8 days after fertilization," which is most common, produces "two embryos, two amnions, one chorion, and one placenta"; division after the eighth day produces "two embryos within a common amnion and a common chorion with one placenta," which "often causes circulatory problems because the umbilical cords may tangle together" (p. 249). Division 13 days or later produces conjoined twins.
q_0342.trap: (D) inverts the latest arrangement, and it inverts the one with the highest stakes — division after day 8 gives the most sharing, not the least, and that is the arrangement carrying cord-entanglement risk.

q_0343.stem: A nurse is reviewing risk factors for twinning. Select all the statements that are accurate.
options: Dizygotic twinning occurs in families and increases with maternal age, peaking at 37 years
Dizygotic twinning can follow discontinuation of oral contraceptives as follicle-stimulating hormone levels rebound
Monozygotic twinning has no association with race, heredity, maternal age, or parity
Assisted reproductive technology increases the incidence of monozygotic twinning by more than tenfold
Monozygotic twinning runs in families in the same way dizygotic twinning does
q_0343.rationale: Dizygotic twinning "occurs in families," is more common among Black women than White women and least common among Asian women, and increases "with maternal age, peaking at 37 years; with parity; with maternal family history of twins; with maternal obesity; and with the use of assisted reproductive technology," as well as after "discontinuation of oral contraceptives as FSH levels rebound." Monozygotic twinning has "no association with race, heredity, maternal age, or parity," though assisted reproductive technology "increases the incidence ... by more than tenfold" (pp. 248–249).
q_0343.trap: (E) is the single wrong option, and it is the clause the fact bank singles out — running in families belongs only to dizygotic twinning, which makes sense mechanically, since what is inherited is the tendency to release more than one ovum. Assisted reproductive technology is the one risk factor that raises both, which is why it cannot be used to tell the two types apart.

q_0344.stem: At a first prenatal visit at 6 weeks, the examiner notes softening of the cervical tip. Which sign does this describe?
options: Goodell sign
Hegar sign
Chadwick sign
Ballottement
q_0344.rationale: "In a normal, unscarred cervix, softening of the cervical tip can be observed about the beginning of the 6th week. This probable sign of pregnancy, the Goodell sign, is due to increased vascularity, slight hypertrophy, and hyperplasia" (p. 253).
q_0344.trap: (B) is the reflex pick because both signs are softening findings at about the same gestational age. The discriminator is which structure: Goodell is the cervix, and Hegar is the lower uterine segment. Two of these three signs are about texture and one is about color, which is the fastest way to sort them.

q_0345.stem: At the same visit, the examiner notes softening and compressibility of the lower uterine segment. Which sign does this describe, and what symptom does the resulting uterine position produce?
options: Hegar sign, which produces exaggerated uterine anteflexion so the fundus presses on the bladder, causing urinary frequency
Goodell sign, which produces cervical friability and postcoital spotting
Chadwick sign, which produces leukorrhea
Hegar sign, which produces painless irregular contractions
q_0345.rationale: "At approximately 6 weeks of gestation, softening and compressibility of the lower uterine segment (uterine isthmus) occurs (Hegar sign)," which "results in exaggerated uterine anteflexion during the first 3 months. In this position, the uterine fundus presses on the urinary bladder, causing the woman to experience urinary frequency" (p. 252).
q_0345.trap: (B) is the mirror error of the previous item, trading the two softening signs. This item also connects the sign to a symptom the patient reports, which is why first-trimester urinary frequency is a mechanical finding rather than an infection until dysuria appears.

q_0346.stem: A patient at 7 weeks has a violet-blue discoloration of the vaginal mucosa and cervix. Which sign is this, and what causes it?
options: Chadwick sign, caused by increased vascularity
Goodell sign, caused by softening of the cervical tip
Hegar sign, caused by compressibility of the isthmus
Melasma, caused by increased melanotropin
q_0346.rationale: "Increased vascularity results in the violet-blue color of the vaginal mucosa and cervix, known as the Chadwick sign. This is evident at 6 to 8 weeks of pregnancy" (p. 253).
q_0346.trap: (B) and (C) are the two texture signs offered against the one color sign, which is how this trio usually appears on an exam. (D) is a real pigmentation change from a later chapter section, but melasma is on the face and appears after week 16, so both site and timing are wrong.

q_0347.stem: During a bimanual examination at 17 weeks, the examiner taps gently upward on the cervix, and the fetus rises and then sinks back against the examining finger. What is this technique called, and who perceives it?
options: Ballottement, perceived by the examiner
Quickening, perceived by the woman
Ballottement, perceived by the woman
Braxton Hicks contractions, perceived by both
q_0347.rationale: Ballottement is the "passive movement of the unengaged fetus," a "technique of palpating a floating structure by bouncing it gently and feeling it rebound," generally possible between 16 and 18 weeks. The examiner "places a finger within the vagina and taps gently upward on the cervix, causing the fetus to rise. The fetus then sinks, and a gentle tap is felt on the finger" (p. 253).
q_0347.trap: (C) keeps the right term and gives it to the wrong person, which is the distinction that matters: ballottement is an examiner's finding and quickening is the woman's. Both occur in roughly the same window, so timing alone cannot separate them.

q_0348.stem: A nulliparous patient at 17 weeks is worried because she has not yet felt fetal movement. Which response is accurate?
options: Quickening occurs at 18 weeks or later in a nulliparous woman, so this is expected
Quickening occurs at 14 to 16 weeks regardless of parity, so evaluation is needed
Quickening occurs at 14 to 16 weeks in a nulliparous woman and later in a multiparous woman
Absence of movement at 17 weeks indicates fetal demise until proven otherwise
q_0348.rationale: Quickening, "the first recognition of fetal movements," occurs at "14 to 16 weeks" in the multiparous woman and at "the 18th week or later" in the nulliparous woman. It is "commonly described as a flutter and is difficult to distinguish from peristalsis," and "the week in which quickening occurs provides a tentative clue in dating the duration of gestation" (p. 253).
q_0348.trap: (C) inverts the parity relationship, which is the error worth catching because it runs the same direction as lightening later in pregnancy — the experienced woman recognizes the finding earlier, and the first-time mother later. A nurse who has the relationship backwards will reassure the wrong patient and alarm the right one.

q_0349.stem: A patient at 20 weeks asks what is making her uterus grow at this stage. Which explanation is accurate?
options: After the third month, uterine enlargement is primarily the result of mechanical pressure of the growing fetus
Uterine enlargement throughout pregnancy is driven entirely by estrogen and progesterone
Uterine enlargement after the third month results from continued hyperplasia of new muscle fibers
Uterine enlargement is caused by increasing amniotic fluid volume alone
q_0349.rationale: "High levels of estrogen and progesterone stimulate significant uterine growth in the first trimester" through increased vascularity, hyperplasia, hypertrophy, and development of the decidua. But "after the third month, uterine enlargement is primarily the result of mechanical pressure of the growing fetus" (p. 252).
q_0349.trap: (B) is the reflex pick because hormones explain so much else in this chapter, and it is wrong specifically because the driver changes partway through. The chapter's two explanatory categories, hormones and mechanical pressure, hand off to each other here, which is why the timing clause matters.

q_0350.stem: A nurse palpating a pregnant abdomen notes that the uterus is rotated to the right. How should this be interpreted?
options: It is expected, probably because of the presence of the rectosigmoid colon on the left side
It is abnormal and suggests a uterine anomaly or an adnexal mass
It is expected, caused by the greater weight of the right-sided placenta
It is abnormal and suggests fetal malposition
q_0350.rationale: "As the uterus enlarges and rises in the abdomen, it rotates to the right, probably because of the presence of the rectosigmoid colon on the left side" (p. 252).
q_0350.trap: (B) treats a normal asymmetry as pathology. The same rightward displacement explains why the renal pelvis and ureter dilate more on the right, which is why right-sided pyelonephritis is the classic presentation in pregnancy — one anatomic fact with two consequences.

q_0351.stem: At which gestational age would the nurse expect to palpate the fundus at the level of the umbilicus?
options: 20 to 22 weeks
12 to 14 weeks
28 to 30 weeks
36 to 38 weeks
q_0351.rationale: The fundus is palpated above the symphysis pubis between the 12th and 14th weeks and "rises gradually to the level of the umbilicus" at 20 to 22 weeks, nearly reaching the xiphoid process at term (p. 252).
q_0351.trap: (B) names the landmark from one row earlier in the same sequence, which is the reliable way this item is missed. The three landmarks are worth learning as a set with their weeks attached, because fundal height is used as a rough dating check at every visit.

q_0352.stem: A nulliparous patient at 38 weeks reports that she is breathing more easily and that her abdomen looks lower. What does this indicate?
options: Lightening, which in a nullipara occurs approximately 2 weeks before the onset of labor
Lightening, which indicates that labor has begun
An abnormal decrease in fundal height requiring immediate evaluation
Braxton Hicks contractions pulling the fundus downward
q_0352.rationale: "Between weeks 38 and 40" the fundal height decreases "as the fetus begins to descend into the pelvis (lightening)." "In general, lightening occurs in the nullipara approximately 2 weeks before the onset of labor and in the multipara at the start of labor" (p. 252).
q_0352.trap: (B) applies the multipara's timing to a nullipara, which would send a woman to the hospital two weeks early. This is the same parity-dependent pattern as quickening: in a first pregnancy the landmark arrives with more warning, and in a later one it arrives closer to the event.

q_0353.stem: A patient at 30 weeks reports irregular, painless tightening of her abdomen that stops when she walks around. Which finding would distinguish these from true labor contractions?
options: True labor contractions increase in intensity and duration and cause cervical dilation; Braxton Hicks contractions do not
True labor contractions are painless, whereas Braxton Hicks contractions are painful
True labor contractions cease with walking, whereas Braxton Hicks contractions intensify with walking
Only the presence of bloody show can distinguish them
q_0353.rationale: Braxton Hicks contractions are "irregular and painless" and "usually cease with walking or exercise." They "can be mistaken for true labor; however, they do not increase in intensity or duration or cause cervical dilation" (p. 253).
q_0353.trap: (C) reverses which contractions stop with activity. The chapter's stated discriminators are progression and cervical change, and cervical change is the one that settles it, because a patient's report of intensity is subjective and the cervix is not.

q_0354.stem: A patient at 30 weeks reports regular abdominal tightening. She has had no cervical examination. What is the priority nursing action?
options: Evaluate for cervical change, because preterm labor contractions can be mistaken for Braxton Hicks contractions, leading to a delay in seeking treatment
Reassure her that these are Braxton Hicks contractions, which are normal after the fourth month
Instruct her to walk, since Braxton Hicks contractions cease with exercise
Schedule her for evaluation at her next routine prenatal visit
q_0354.rationale: The chapter states the danger in both directions: Braxton Hicks contractions can be mistaken for true labor, and "conversely, preterm labor contractions can be mistaken for Braxton Hicks contractions, which can lead to a delay in seeking treatment" (p. 253).
q_0354.trap: (B) is the plausible reassurance, and it is exactly the error the source names. At 30 weeks the cost of wrongly reassuring is preterm birth, so the reasoning has to run toward evaluation rather than toward the reassuring explanation, however common that explanation is.

q_0355.stem: On auscultation of a pregnant abdomen the nurse hears a rushing sound synchronous with the maternal pulse. What is this, and what would a sound synchronous with the fetal heart rate be?
options: The uterine souffle, maternal blood flowing through the uterine arteries; a funic souffle is fetal blood coursing through the umbilical cord
The funic souffle, maternal blood in the uterine arteries; a uterine souffle is fetal blood in the cord
The uterine souffle, fetal blood in the umbilical cord; a funic souffle is maternal in origin
A systolic ejection murmur transmitted from the maternal heart
q_0355.rationale: The uterine souffle is "a rushing or blowing sound of maternal blood flowing through uterine arteries to the placenta that is synchronous with the maternal pulse," while the funic souffle "is synchronous with the fetal heart rate and is caused by fetal blood coursing through the umbilical cord" (p. 253).
q_0355.trap: (B) swaps the two names, which is the entire content of this item — the sounds are told apart by which pulse they match, and matching the wrong one reverses whose circulation is being heard.

q_0356.stem: A patient at 24 weeks has a blood pressure lower than her prepregnancy baseline, although her cardiac output has increased substantially. Which explanation is accurate?
options: Systemic vascular resistance decreases by 30% to 50% because of the vasodilatory effects of progesterone, prostaglandins, and relaxin
Cardiac output does not actually rise in pregnancy; the measurement is unreliable
Blood pressure falls because blood volume decreases in the second trimester
Blood pressure falls because maternal heart rate decreases in pregnancy
q_0356.rationale: "Although CO increases significantly during pregnancy, maternal blood pressure remains the same or decreases slightly. This is due to reduced SVR caused primarily by the vasodilatory effects of progesterone, prostaglandins, and relaxin." Systemic vascular resistance "decreases by 30% to 50% and is lowest at 16 to 34 weeks" (p. 256).
q_0356.trap: (C) and (D) both invert a real pregnancy change: blood volume rises 40% to 45% and heart rate rises 10 to 20 beats per minute. The apparent paradox resolves only through resistance, and the diastolic nadir at 24 to 32 weeks is why a "normal" second-trimester reading can conceal developing hypertension.

q_0357.stem: A patient's blood pressure readings have varied across three prenatal visits. Which factor should the nurse consider first?
options: Position, since brachial blood pressure is highest sitting, lowest in the lateral recumbent position, and intermediate supine
Time of day only, since circadian rhythm is the dominant influence
Cuff size only, since arm circumference changes little in pregnancy
Position is irrelevant to brachial readings in pregnancy
q_0357.rationale: "Brachial blood pressure is highest when the woman is sitting, lowest when she is lying in the lateral recumbent position, and intermediate when she is supine" (p. 256). Age, activity level, health problems, circadian rhythm, alcohol, smoking, anxiety, and pain also influence readings.
q_0357.trap: (D) is the assumption behind most inconsistent prenatal blood pressures. Because the three positions produce a predictable ordering, a reading taken in a different position from the last one can look like a trend when it is only a posture change.

q_0358.stem: A patient at 30 weeks becomes lightheaded and faint several minutes after lying flat for an ultrasound. Which finding would the nurse expect, and what is the intervention?
options: A reflex bradycardia with cardiac output reduced by half; reposition her to the left lateral position
A reflex tachycardia with cardiac output increased; elevate her legs while she remains supine
A rise in blood pressure from aortic compression; place her in a sitting position
No physiologic change; her symptoms are most likely anxiety
q_0358.rationale: "After 4 to 5 minutes, a reflex bradycardia is noted, CO is reduced by half, and the woman feels faint. This condition is called supine hypotensive syndrome or vena cava syndrome." Cardiac output falls "as much as 25% to 30%" when a pregnant woman turns from left lateral recumbent to supine, and some women drop more than 30 mm Hg systolic (p. 256).
q_0358.trap: (B) substitutes tachycardia for bradycardia, which is the compensation a reader expects rather than the one the book describes. Getting this backwards matters because a bradycardic, faint pregnant patient who is lying flat needs repositioning, not a workup.

q_0359.stem: A patient at 34 weeks reports ankle edema, leg varicosities, and hemorrhoids. Which explanation should the nurse give?
options: Compression of the iliac veins and inferior vena cava by the uterus raises venous pressure and reduces blood flow in the legs except in the lateral position
These findings indicate preeclampsia and require immediate evaluation
These findings result from increased systemic vascular resistance in the third trimester
These findings indicate venous thromboembolism until proven otherwise
q_0359.rationale: "Compression of the iliac veins and inferior vena cava by the uterus causes increased venous pressure and reduced blood flow in the legs except when the woman is in the lateral position," producing "dependent edema, varicose veins in the legs and vulva, and hemorrhoids" and contributing to "the increased risk for venous thromboembolism" (p. 256).
q_0359.trap: (B) escalates a mechanical, positional finding into a hypertensive disorder. Dependent edema in the legs is expected; what would change the picture is hypertension with proteinuria, which this stem does not supply.

q_0360.stem: On auscultation of a patient at 28 weeks, the nurse hears splitting of the first and second heart sounds, a third heart sound, and a systolic ejection murmur at the left sternal border. How should these be interpreted?
options: All are expected findings in pregnancy and are transient, usually disappearing shortly after birth
A systolic ejection murmur is always pathologic and requires echocardiography
A third heart sound in pregnancy indicates fluid overload requiring diuresis
These findings indicate cardiac decompensation and require immediate referral
q_0360.rationale: "By the end of the first trimester, there is an audible splitting" of the first and second heart sounds. "The majority of pregnant women also have a third heart sound after midpregnancy resulting from rapid diastolic filling. Approximately 96% of women develop systolic ejection murmurs that are most audible over the left sternal border." "The auscultatory changes are transient and usually disappear shortly after birth" (p. 256).
q_0360.trap: (C) is the reflex from adult cardiac assessment, where a third heart sound suggests failure. In pregnancy it is present in the majority of women from rapid diastolic filling, and treating it as overload could lead to a diuretic — which this chapter separately warns causes severe hypovolemia and reduced placental perfusion.

q_0361.stem: A patient at 26 weeks has a hemoglobin of 10.8 g/dL. How should the nurse interpret this?
options: It is within normal limits for the second trimester, where anemia is defined as hemoglobin less than 10.5 g/dL
It indicates anemia, since the threshold is 11 g/dL in every trimester
It indicates anemia and requires transfusion
It cannot be interpreted without a serum ferritin level
q_0361.rationale: A pregnant woman is anemic with "hemoglobin less than 11 g/dL or hematocrit less than 33%" in the first or third trimester, and with "hemoglobin less than 10.5 g/dL or hematocrit less than 32%" in the second trimester (p. 257).
q_0361.trap: (B) applies the first- and third-trimester cutoff to a second-trimester patient, which labels a normal value as anemia. The threshold is lower in the second trimester precisely because that is when hemodilution is most pronounced — the physiology and the cutoff move together.

q_0362.stem: A patient asks why her hemoglobin is lower than before pregnancy if she is being told her blood count is normal. Which explanation is accurate?
options: Plasma volume increases faster than red blood cell production, producing hemodilution called physiologic anemia; red cell mass itself rises 20% to 30%
Red blood cell production decreases in pregnancy, which is why the hemoglobin falls
The hemoglobin falls because iron is diverted entirely to the fetus
The finding is always pathologic and indicates iron deficiency
q_0362.rationale: "Because the plasma increase is greater than the increase in RBC production, there is a decrease in the normal hemoglobin and hematocrit values. This state of hemodilution is referred to as physiologic anemia of pregnancy," which is "more noticeable during the second trimester." Red cell mass increases "250 to 450 mL, or approximately 20% to 30% over prepregnancy values," and the percentage of increase "depends on the amount of iron available" (p. 257).
q_0362.trap: (B) is the intuitive misreading of a falling hemoglobin — that the marrow must be making fewer cells. Red cell mass genuinely rises; it is simply outpaced by plasma, which is why the finding is a dilution rather than a production problem.

q_0363.stem: A pregnant patient at 30 weeks has a white blood cell count of 14,000 per cubic millimeter. She is afebrile with no localizing symptoms. How should the nurse interpret this?
options: It is within the expected range for pregnancy, where the white count ranges from 5000 to 15,000
It indicates infection and requires cultures and antibiotics
It indicates a hematologic malignancy and requires referral
It is below the expected pregnancy range and suggests immunosuppression
q_0363.rationale: Table 13.2 gives a pregnant white blood cell range of 5000 to 15,000 per cubic millimeter, against a nonpregnant 5000 to 10,000. The count "begins to increase as early as the 2nd month," primarily in granulocytes, nonclassic monocytes, and polymorphonuclear leukocytes, while "the lymphocyte count stays approximately the same" (p. 257).
q_0363.trap: (B) applies a nonpregnant reference range, which is the practical error this table exists to prevent. An elevated white count is not by itself evidence of infection in pregnancy, so the febrile and localizing findings, absent here, are what would carry the diagnosis.

q_0364.stem: A nurse is reviewing expected laboratory changes in pregnancy. Select all the statements that are accurate.
options: Fibrinogen increases from a nonpregnant 200 to 400 mg/dL to a pregnant 400 to 650 mg/dL
Platelet count shows no significant change
Fasting blood glucose decreases relative to nonpregnant values
Hematocrit is expected to be above 33%
Platelet count decreases markedly, which is why bleeding risk rises
q_0364.rationale: Table 13.2 gives fibrinogen as 400 to 650 mg/dL in pregnancy against a nonpregnant 200 to 400; platelets as "no significant change"; fasting glucose as 60 to 105 mg/dL against a nonpregnant 70 to 110; and hematocrit as above 33% (p. 257).
q_0364.trap: (E) is the single wrong option, and it inverts the direction of pregnancy's coagulation change in both halves. Platelets do not fall, and pregnancy is a hypercoagulable rather than a bleeding-prone state, so the option is wrong about the value and about what it would mean.

q_0365.stem: A patient asks why pregnancy increases her risk of blood clots. Which explanation is accurate?
options: Clotting factors VII, VIII, IX, and X and fibrinogen increase, inhibitors such as protein S decrease, and fibrinolytic activity is depressed, producing a five- to sixfold increased risk
Platelet count and function increase markedly, producing a hypercoagulable state
Clotting factors II and V increase while all other factors remain unchanged
Pregnancy is a hypocoagulable state, and clot risk rises only after birth
q_0365.rationale: "Pregnancy is considered a hypercoagulable state in which women are at a five- to sixfold increased risk for thromboembolic problems," through "increases in various clotting factors (i.e., factors VII, VIII, IX, and X and fibrinogen) and decreases in factors that inhibit coagulation (e.g., protein S)," while "fibrinolytic activity ... is depressed." This "provides a protective function to decrease the chance of bleeding but also makes the woman more vulnerable to thrombosis, especially after cesarean birth" (p. 257).
q_0365.trap: (C) names the wrong factors, which the fact bank flags as the checkable error in this list. (B) reaches for platelets, which the same table says do not significantly change — the hypercoagulability is a plasma-factor phenomenon, not a platelet one.

q_0366.stem: A nurse is reviewing expected respiratory changes in pregnancy. Select all the statements that are accurate.
options: Respiratory rate is unchanged or only slightly increased
Tidal volume increases by approximately 40%
Minute ventilation increases by 30% to 50%
Expiratory reserve volume decreases by approximately 20%
Vital capacity decreases markedly as the diaphragm rises
q_0366.rationale: Table 13.3 gives respiratory rate as "unchanged or slightly increased," tidal volume increased 40%, vital capacity "unchanged," inspiratory capacity increased 6%, expiratory reserve volume decreased 20%, total lung capacity "unchanged to slightly decreased," minute ventilation increased 30% to 50%, and oxygen consumption increased 20% to 40% (p. 258).
q_0366.trap: (E) is the single wrong option and it is the one that intuition supplies: the diaphragm does rise as much as 4 cm, so vital capacity ought to fall. It does not, because the costal angle increases and the transverse thoracic diameter widens by about 2 cm, compensating — which is why total lung capacity is also nearly unchanged.

q_0367.stem: A patient at 28 weeks reports feeling short of breath at rest, which began in the second trimester. She has no orthopnea, chest pain, or edema beyond mild ankle swelling. How should the nurse interpret this?
options: This is consistent with physiologic dyspnea of pregnancy, which occurs with mild exertion or at rest and begins in the first or second trimester
Dyspnea at rest is never physiologic and always indicates cardiac decompensation
Physiologic dyspnea begins only in the third trimester, so this requires evaluation
This indicates pulmonary embolism until proven otherwise
q_0367.rationale: "Pregnancy-related dyspnea is common, beginning in the first or second trimester. This physiologic dyspnea occurs with mild exertion or at rest." The chapter adds that it is "important to differentiate physiologic from pathologic dyspnea, such as may be caused by cardiac decompensation" (p. 257).
q_0367.trap: (B) is the reflex escalation, and it is wrong on the specific point that separates the two patterns — physiologic dyspnea does occur at rest, so "at rest" is not the discriminator. Onset in the first or second trimester without other cardiac findings is the reassuring pattern.

q_0368.stem: An arterial blood gas on a healthy pregnant patient shows a decreased PaCO2, decreased bicarbonate, and a slightly increased pH. How should the nurse interpret this?
options: A compensated respiratory alkalosis, which is the expected acid-base state of pregnancy
A metabolic alkalosis caused by vomiting earlier in pregnancy
A respiratory acidosis caused by upward displacement of the diaphragm
A laboratory error, since pregnancy does not alter acid-base balance
q_0368.rationale: "Pregnancy is a state of chronic mild hyperventilation with reduced arterial carbon dioxide and increased oxygen over nonpregnant levels." "Progesterone may be responsible for increasing the sensitivity of the respiratory center receptors so that PaCO2 decreases, the base excess (bicarbonate) decreases, and pH increases slightly. These alterations in acid-base balance create a state of respiratory alkalosis" (p. 257).
q_0368.trap: (C) reasons from the mechanical change to the wrong direction: the diaphragm does rise, but ventilation increases rather than falls, so carbon dioxide is blown off rather than retained. Naming it metabolic, as (B) does, misses that the primary change is in carbon dioxide.

q_0369.stem: What purpose does the maternal respiratory alkalosis of pregnancy serve for the fetus?
options: It facilitates transport of carbon dioxide from the fetus to the mother and release of oxygen from the mother to the fetus
It increases maternal oxygen storage for use during labor
It prevents fetal respiratory acidosis by raising fetal carbon dioxide
It has no fetal purpose and is an incidental consequence of progesterone
q_0369.rationale: The acid-base changes "also facilitate the transport of CO2 from the fetus to the mother and O2 release from the mother to the fetus" (p. 257). Maternal oxygen consumption rises steadily, reaching 40% above nonpregnant levels by term.
q_0369.trap: (D) is the pick for anyone who has learned the change without the reason. The gradient the alkalosis creates is what allows a placenta working by diffusion to move gases in both directions efficiently, which connects this chapter to the fetal oxygenation adaptations in Chapter 12.

q_0370.stem: A patient in the third trimester reports worsening heartburn. Which mechanism should the nurse describe?
options: Increased progesterone decreases the tone and motility of smooth muscle, causing reflux, slower gastric emptying, and reverse peristalsis
Increased estrogen causes hypersecretion of hydrochloric acid
The enlarging uterus compresses the esophagus directly
Gastric emptying accelerates in pregnancy, forcing acid upward
q_0370.rationale: "Increased progesterone causes decreased tone and motility of smooth muscles," resulting in reflux, "slower emptying time of the stomach, and reverse peristalsis." The woman "may experience acid indigestion, or heartburn (pyrosis), beginning as early as the first trimester and intensifying through the third trimester" (p. 258).
q_0370.trap: (D) reverses the motility change, and (B) reaches for the wrong hormone — Table 13.4 in fact credits estrogen with *decreasing* secretion of hydrochloric acid and pepsin. The chapter's discipline is to answer "why" with the mechanism it names, and for gastrointestinal smooth muscle that mechanism is progesterone.

q_0371.stem: A pregnant patient at 32 weeks has suspected appendicitis. Where would the nurse expect her pain to localize?
options: High and to the right, in the right upper quadrant, because the appendix is displaced upward and laterally away from the McBurney point
At the McBurney point in the right lower quadrant, as in a nonpregnant patient
In the left lower quadrant, because the uterus rotates to the right and displaces the appendix leftward
Diffusely across the lower abdomen with no localization
q_0371.rationale: The appendix is "displaced upward and laterally, high and to the right, away from the McBurney point," which makes appendicitis "difficult to diagnose in pregnancy" (p. 258).
q_0371.trap: (B) is the answer a nonpregnant assessment would give, and it is the reason appendicitis is missed in pregnancy. The displacement is mechanical and progressive, so the later the gestation, the further from the expected location the pain will be.

q_0372.stem: A patient at 7 weeks reports nausea that is worst in the evening. She asks whether this means something is wrong, since it is called morning sickness. Which response is accurate?
options: Only about half of women have symptoms in the morning; for some it is worse in the evening and for others constant, and it typically peaks at 8 to 12 weeks and subsides by the end of the first trimester
Evening nausea is atypical and suggests a gastrointestinal disorder
Nausea beginning at 7 weeks is late and should be evaluated
Nausea that is not worst in the morning indicates hyperemesis gravidarum
q_0372.rationale: Up to 80% of pregnant women experience nausea with or without vomiting. "Although ... commonly referred to as 'morning sickness,' only about half of the women experience the symptoms in the morning. For some, it is worse in the evening, and others experience symptoms constantly." It "generally appears at 4 to 6 weeks of gestation, peaks by 8 to 12 weeks, and usually subsides by the end of the first trimester" (p. 258).
q_0372.trap: (D) reaches for the complication on the strength of an atypical timing that the source explicitly calls typical. The escalation criteria are different ones entirely, and confusing "not in the morning" with "severe" would send a normally progressing patient for an unnecessary workup.

q_0373.stem: Which pattern of nausea and vomiting in pregnancy warrants further evaluation?
options: Vomiting that is severe, persists beyond the first trimester, or is accompanied by fever, pain, or weight loss
Any vomiting occurring more than once daily in the first trimester
Nausea that is worse in the evening than in the morning
Nausea accompanied by an increased appetite in the second trimester
q_0373.rationale: "Rarely does NVP have harmful effects on the embryo, fetus, or woman. When the vomiting is severe or persists beyond the first trimester or when it is accompanied by fever, pain, or weight loss, further evaluation is necessary, and medical intervention is often needed. The diagnosis of hyperemesis gravidarum is likely in such cases" (p. 258).
q_0373.trap: (D) describes a normal finding — "by the end of the second trimester, the appetite increases in response to increasing metabolic needs" — dressed up as a warning sign. The three escalation criteria are duration, severity, and the accompanying findings, and none of them is frequency alone.

q_0374.stem: A pregnant patient develops pyelonephritis. Why is the right side affected more often, and what predisposes her to infection at all?
options: The renal pelvis and ureter dilate more on the right because the heavy uterus is displaced to the right by the sigmoid colon, and the resulting urinary stasis increases susceptibility
The right ureter is naturally shorter, and pregnancy has no effect on urinary stasis
The left side dilates more, and the right-sided presentation reflects referred pain
Susceptibility increases because glomerular filtration rate falls in pregnancy
q_0374.rationale: "In the latter part of pregnancy, the renal pelvis and ureter dilate more on the right side than on the left because the heavy uterus is displaced to the right by the sigmoid colon." The consequence is that "a larger volume of urine is held in the pelves and ureters, and urine flow rate is slowed, causing urinary stasis. ... Because of urinary stasis and potential stagnation, pregnant women are more susceptible to urinary tract infections" (p. 259).
