q_0849.rationale: The Safety Alert states: "Magnesium sulfate is contraindicated in women with myasthenia gravis because it inhibits the release of acetylcholine and can trigger myasthenic crisis." Myasthenia gravis is "an autoimmune motor (muscle) end-plate disorder that involves acetylcholine use."
q_0849.trap: (A) is correct for nearly every other woman with preeclampsia, which is what makes this pairing worth holding as an absolute. Because myasthenia gravis does not affect smooth muscle, most women tolerate labor well, though vacuum or forceps assistance may be required and regional analgesia is preferred.

q_0850.stem: A newborn of a mother with myasthenia gravis has a weak cry, difficulty suckling, a weak Moro reflex, and feeble limb movements at 24 hours of age. What is this, and what is the course?
options: Neonatal myasthenia, affecting approximately 10% to 15% of these newborns, from transfer of maternal antibodies against acetylcholine receptors, appearing within the first 72 hours, treatable with anticholinesterase medications and usually resolving by 6 weeks
Permanent congenital myasthenia gravis
Neonatal abstinence syndrome
Birth asphyxia
q_0850.rationale: "Approximately 10% to 15% of neonates born to women with MG develop neonatal myasthenia," which "results from the transfer of maternal antibodies against acetylcholine receptors across the placenta." Symptoms "usually appear within the first 72 hours after birth" and the disorder "can be treated with anticholinesterase medications and usually resolves by 6 weeks after birth."
q_0850.trap: (B) treats a transient antibody-mediated condition as an inherited one, which would change everything a family is told about their baby's future.

q_0851.topic: gastrointestinal and hepatic disorders in pregnancy
q_0851.stem: A woman at 24 weeks has epigastric and right upper quadrant pain radiating to her back after a high-fat meal, with nausea, vomiting, and fever, and the pain is severe and prolonged. Which condition does this describe?
options: Cholelithiasis alone, since gallstones cause pain after fatty meals
Cholecystitis, inflammation of the gallbladder usually caused when a gallstone obstructs a cystic duct, in which the pain is more severe and prolonged and nausea, vomiting, and fever may be present
Appendicitis
Preeclampsia
q_0851.rationale: Cholelithiasis is "the presence of gallstones in the gallbladder," with biliary colic as the usual first symptom, occurring spontaneously or after a high-fat meal. Cholecystitis "is usually caused when a gallstone obstructs a cystic duct," and its pain "is usually more severe and prolonged," with nausea, vomiting, and fever.
q_0851.trap: (A) stops at the stones. The distinction drives management: cholelithiasis is often managed conservatively with surgery postponed until postpartum, while "women with recurrent biliary colic or acute cholecystitis generally require immediate cholecystectomy."

q_0852.topic: gastrointestinal and hepatic disorders in pregnancy
q_0852.stem: A cholecystectomy is planned during pregnancy. What does the chapter say about timing and technique?
options: The second trimester has traditionally been considered safest, but the surgery is increasingly performed at any time during pregnancy, and laparoscopic cholecystectomy is the preferred procedure
Surgery is never performed during pregnancy
Only open cholecystectomy is safe in pregnancy
Surgery is performed only in the first trimester
q_0852.rationale: "Although the second trimester has traditionally been considered the safest time for this surgery, it is increasingly performed at any time during pregnancy because of improved surgical techniques and outcomes. While both laparoscopic and open cholecystectomy can safely be performed in all trimesters, laparoscopic cholecystectomy is the preferred procedure."
q_0852.trap: (C) is the older teaching, and cholecystitis is "the third most common indication for nonobstetric surgical intervention in pregnancy."

q_0853.topic: gastrointestinal and hepatic disorders in pregnancy
q_0853.stem: Which dietary instructions belong in nutritional counseling for a pregnant woman with cholelithiasis or cholecystitis? Select all that apply.
options: Assess your diet for foods that cause discomfort and gas, and omit foods that trigger episodes
Limit dietary fat intake to 40 to 50 g/day
Limit protein to 10% to 12% of total calories, with most calories from carbohydrates
Prepare food without adding fats or oils as much as possible, and avoid fried foods
Increase dietary fat to slow gallbladder emptying
q_0853.rationale: The Teaching for Self-Management box lists identifying and omitting trigger foods, limiting fat to 40 to 50 g/day, limiting protein to 10% to 12% of calories with most calories from carbohydrates, preparing food without added fats or oils, and avoiding fried foods.
q_0853.trap: (E) inverts the central instruction. Fat is what stimulates gallbladder contraction, which is why the pain classically follows a high-fat meal.

q_0854.topic: gastrointestinal and hepatic disorders in pregnancy
q_0854.stem: A woman with Crohn disease becomes pregnant and asks whether to stop her medications. What does the chapter direct?
options: Stop all medications during the first trimester

Continue them, because discontinuing prepregnancy medications can cause a relapse or disease flare, and the drugs used appear to be safe during pregnancy; folic acid 2 to 4 mg daily and calcium supplementation are recommended
Switch to over-the-counter remedies
Stop only the corticosteroids
q_0854.rationale: "Discontinuing her prepregnancy medications can cause the woman to have a relapse or disease flare," and the drugs named — 5-aminosalicylates, prednisone, 6-mercaptopurine or azathioprine, occasionally biologics, and metronidazole or ciprofloxacin — "appear to be safe for use during pregnancy." A daily dose of 2 to 4 mg of folic acid "counteracts the antifolate actions of some medications," and calcium supplementation is necessary "because osteoporosis is a significant complication in up to one-third of these women."
q_0854.trap: (A) is the reflex response to any medication in pregnancy, and here it creates the flare that itself raises the risk of preterm birth, low birth weight, and small-for-gestational-age infants.

q_0855.topic: gastrointestinal and hepatic disorders in pregnancy
q_0855.stem: A woman at 32 weeks reports intense generalized itching, worst at night and involving her palms and soles, with no rash. What should the nurse suspect, and what is the treatment?
options: Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy, with no skin lesions present, elevated serum bile acids and liver function tests, treated with ursodeoxycholic acid
Polymorphic eruption of pregnancy, treated with topical steroids
A drug allergy
Scabies
q_0855.rationale: Intrahepatic cholestasis "is characterized by generalized pruritus that usually begins in the third trimester," with "no skin lesions present," itching that "commonly affects the palms and soles" and is "usually worse at night," elevated serum bile acids and liver function tests, and treatment with ursodeoxycholic acid. Birth at approximately 37 weeks should be considered, and it recurs in 40% to 90% of later pregnancies.
q_0855.trap: (B) names a condition with a rash, and the absence of skin lesions is the discriminator. Fetal complications include asphyxial events, meconium staining, stillbirth, and preterm birth, which is why the timing of birth matters.

q_0856.stem: A routine first-visit urine culture in an asymptomatic woman grows 120,000 organisms/mL. How is this classified and managed, and what happens if it is untreated?
options: Asymptomatic bacteriuria; it is treated with antibiotics, because if untreated about one-third of pregnant women will develop acute pyelonephritis
Contamination; the specimen is repeated and no treatment is given
Cystitis; it is treated with a 3-day course
It requires no treatment because she has no symptoms
q_0856.rationale: "A clean-voided urine specimen containing more than 100,000 organisms/mL is diagnostic" of asymptomatic bacteriuria, and "all women should be screened for asymptomatic bacteriuria at their first prenatal visit." Treatment regimens may be single-dose or 3, 7, or 10 days. "If asymptomatic bacteriuria is not treated, about one-third of pregnant women will develop acute pyelonephritis," and it is also associated with preterm birth and low birth weight.
q_0856.trap: (D) is the reasoning the screening program exists to override — the absence of symptoms is what defines the diagnosis, not what excludes it.

q_0857.stem: A pregnant woman reports dysuria, urgency, frequency, and suprapubic pain, with microscopic hematuria and no fever or flank pain. Which condition is this, and how is it treated?
options: Cystitis, in which symptoms are confined to the bladder rather than becoming systemic, often treated with a 3-day course of antibiotics that is usually 90% effective
Pyelonephritis, treated with IV antibiotics
Asymptomatic bacteriuria
Vaginitis
q_0857.rationale: "Cystitis (bladder infection) is characterized by dysuria, urgency, and frequency, along with lower abdominal or suprapubic pain," with white blood cells and bacteria in the urine and possible microscopic or gross hematuria, and "symptoms are confined to the bladder rather than becoming systemic." It is "often treated with a 3-day course of antibiotic therapy, which is usually 90% effective."
q_0857.trap: (B) is the next rung up and is distinguished by systemic findings — fever, chills, flank pain, and costovertebral angle tenderness — none of which this stem gives.

q_0858.stem: A woman at 28 weeks has an abrupt onset of fever, chills, right flank pain, nausea and vomiting, and right costovertebral angle tenderness. Which statements about her condition are accurate? Select all that apply.
options: Pyelonephritis is the most frequent serious nonobstetric medical complication of pregnancy and a leading cause of septic shock during pregnancy
Infection develops only in the right kidney in more than half of all cases
IV antibiotics are begun as soon as cultures are collected, with ceftriaxone often prescribed
IV fluids are given to maintain urine output at 50 mL or more per hour
She may be discharged as soon as her fever begins to fall, without completing antibiotics
q_0858.rationale: Pyelonephritis presents abruptly with fever, chills, flank pain, dysuria, urgency, and frequency, with one or both costovertebral angles tender; it develops only in the right kidney in more than half of cases; IV antibiotics begin once cultures are collected; and urine output is maintained at 50 mL/h or more. Women are hospitalized 12 to 24 hours for assessment before a decision about outpatient management.
q_0858.trap: (E) contradicts the discharge criterion — "once a woman has been afebrile and asymptomatic for 24 hours" — and the 14-day outpatient course. More than 20% of women remain febrile for more than 4 days, and recurrent bacteriuria develops in 30% to 40% after treatment.

q_0859.stem: A woman prescribed phenazopyridine along with her antibiotic should be taught which of the following?
options: That the medication colors urine and tears orange, that she should avoid wearing contact lenses while taking it, and that it will stain underwear
That it replaces the antibiotic once symptoms improve
That it must be taken on an empty stomach
That orange urine indicates an allergic reaction
q_0859.rationale: Phenazopyridine is "a urinary analgesic" given with the antibiotic for symptom relief, and the teaching is that "the medication colors urine and tears orange," so women should "avoid wearing contact lenses while taking this medication" and be "warned that it will stain underwear."
q_0859.trap: (D) turns an expected effect into an emergency, and (B) is the more dangerous error: relief of symptoms is exactly when women stop antibiotics, and "failure to complete treatment can lead to the creation of additional drug-resistant organisms."

q_0860.stem: Which statements about diagnosing appendicitis in pregnancy are accurate? Select all that apply.
options: The most common symptom is right lower quadrant abdominal pain, regardless of gestational age
As pregnancy progresses the appendix is pushed upward and to the right
The white blood cell count is not helpful because of the physiologic increase in WBCs in pregnancy
Loss of appetite is not a reliable indicator
An elevated white blood cell count confirms the diagnosis
q_0860.rationale: "The most common symptom of appendicitis in pregnant women is right lower quadrant abdominal pain, regardless of gestational age." The appendix is displaced upward and to the right, loss of appetite "is not a reliable indicator," and "because of the physiologic increase in WBCs that occurs in pregnancy, this test is not helpful in making the diagnosis." Fever, tachycardia, dry tongue, and localized tenderness are less likely indicators than in nonpregnant patients.
q_0860.trap: (E) uses a real laboratory value to say nothing, and it is the option that most feels like clinical confirmation. Rupture occurs in up to 40% of pregnant women with appendicitis, largely because the diagnosis is delayed.

q_0861.stem: Which imaging sequence does the chapter recommend for suspected appendicitis in pregnancy?
options: CT first, as in nonpregnant clients
Ultrasonography first to avoid fetal radiation exposure from CT, with MRI as the appropriate next step if appendicitis has not been confirmed
MRI first, then CT
Plain abdominal radiography
q_0861.rationale: CT "is the imaging test of choice in nonpregnant clients," but "the use of ultrasonography during pregnancy is preferred to avoid fetal exposure to radiation from CT," and "magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is the appropriate next step in a pregnant woman if appendicitis has not been confirmed by other imaging techniques." A urinalysis and chest x-ray are done to rule out UTI and right lower lobe pneumonia.
q_0861.trap: (A) applies the nonpregnant standard, which is exactly the reasoning the chapter corrects.

q_0862.stem: A pregnant woman requires urgent nonobstetric surgery. Which perioperative measures does the chapter specify? Select all that apply.
options: Encouraging her to express her fears, concerns, and questions
A complete blood count with differential and urinalysis at minimum, with FHR and uterine activity monitored
Special precautions such as administering an antacid before anesthesia, because an unexpected surgical patient is in danger of vomiting and aspirating even if she has had nothing by mouth
Positioning on the operating table with a lateral tilt to avoid compression of the maternal vena cava
Withholding all fetal monitoring until 24 hours after surgery
q_0862.rationale: The chapter names expressing fears as an important aspect of preoperative care, the minimum laboratory set with fetal and uterine monitoring, the aspiration precaution for unexpected surgery, and the lateral tilt intraoperatively to improve fetal oxygenation. Continuous monitoring during surgery may be performed if the fetus is viable, using sterile gel and a sterile transducer sleeve, though many practitioners monitor before and after only.
q_0862.trap: (E) contradicts postoperative practice, where monitoring is "likely to be initiated or resumed because of the potential risk for preterm labor," with tocolysis if preterm labor occurs.

q_0863.stem: Which items belong in discharge teaching after nonobstetric surgery during pregnancy, per Box 30.2? Select all that apply.
options: Care of the incision site, and diet and elimination related to gastrointestinal function
Signs and symptoms of wound infection, venous thromboembolism, and pneumonia
Equipment needed and technique for assessing temperature
Assessment of fetal activity with kick counts, and signs of preterm labor, if birth has not occurred
Instructions to resume full activity immediately
q_0863.rationale: Box 30.2 lists incision care, diet and elimination, complication signs, temperature assessment, a recommended schedule for resuming activities of daily living, treatments and medications, resource people and telephone numbers, follow-up visits, and — if birth has not occurred — kick counts and signs of preterm labor.
q_0863.trap: (E) replaces a graded schedule with an unrestricted one. Home care planning "should be completed as early as possible before discharge," with supervised practice for the woman and caregivers.

q_0864.stem: A pregnant woman at 30 weeks arrives after a motor vehicle crash, unstable and bleeding. A team member moves to apply the fetal monitor first. What does the chapter direct?
options: Fetal assessment first, since the fetus is more vulnerable
Resuscitate the woman and stabilize her condition first, then consider fetal needs, because fetal survival depends on maternal survival
Simultaneous equal priority for mother and fetus
Immediate cesarean birth before any resuscitation
q_0864.rationale: The Safety Alert states: "Priorities of care for the pregnant woman after trauma must be to resuscitate the woman and stabilize her condition first and then consider fetal needs." The chapter notes that "the initial response of many trauma team members ... is to assess fetal status first," and corrects it: "fetal survival depends on maternal survival, and stabilizing the pregnant woman improves the chance of fetal survival." Pregnancy "should not result in any restriction of the usual diagnostic, pharmacologic, or resuscitative procedures."
q_0864.trap: (A) is the instinct the chapter names and then overrules, and (D) skips resuscitation entirely for a procedure that depends on it.

q_0865.stem: How is the airway established in a pregnant trauma patient, and what else does the primary survey include?
options: Jaw thrust, because hyperextension of the neck is avoided and cervical spine injury is always assumed; the sequence is the CABDs — compressions, airway, breathing, and defibrillation
Head tilt-chin lift with full neck extension
Immediate intubation without cervical precautions
Airway management is deferred until after fetal assessment
q_0865.rationale: The Safety Alert directs: "Hyperextension of the neck is avoided; instead, jaw thrust is used to establish an airway for the pregnant trauma survivor." The chapter's mnemonic for the primary survey is "the initial CABDs of resuscitation: compressions, airway, breathing, and defibrillation," and "the presence of a cervical spine injury is always assumed."
q_0865.trap: (B) is the correct maneuver in the cardiac-arrest algorithm — the CPR box does direct head tilt-chin lift — but not in a trauma patient with a presumed cervical spine injury.

q_0866.stem: Which measures does the chapter specify for stabilizing a pregnant trauma patient? Select all that apply.
options: Supplemental oxygen by tight-fitting nonrebreathing mask at 10 to 12 L/min
Two large-bore, 14- to 16-gauge intravenous lines
Normal saline for quick volume expansion, with low-volume resuscitation now recommended to avoid fluid overload
Positioning the uterus to one side after 20 weeks, or manual deflection or a wedge under one side of the backboard
Vasopressors as the first-line treatment for hypotension
q_0866.rationale: The chapter specifies oxygen at 10 to 12 L/min by tight-fitting nonrebreathing mask, two large-bore IV lines, normal saline with low-volume resuscitation because large crystalloid volumes cause tissue edema, ARDS, dilutional coagulopathy, and regulatory disruption, and lateral uterine positioning after 20 weeks. Blood products are given in a 1:1:1 ratio of platelets, plasma, and packed red cells.
q_0866.trap: (E) reverses two rules at once: "hypovolemia should be presumed to be the cause of hypotension until proven otherwise," and "administering vasopressor drugs to treat maternal hypotension should be avoided if possible" because they reduce uterine blood flow.

q_0867.stem: Which modifications to cardiopulmonary resuscitation are specific to pregnancy? Select all that apply.
options: Left lateral uterine displacement if the fundal height is at or above the umbilicus, indicating approximately 20 weeks of gestation
Chest compressions performed slightly higher on the sternum if the enlarged uterus has displaced the diaphragm upward
Defibrillator paddles placed one rib interspace higher than usual
A compression rate reduced to 80/min because of the pregnancy
A compression-to-ventilation ratio changed to 15:2
q_0867.rationale: The three pregnancy-specific modifications are lateral uterine displacement at or above 20 weeks, compressions slightly higher on the sternum, and paddles one interspace higher because "the heart is displaced slightly by the enlarged uterus." Uterine displacement is critical because cardiac output from compressions, already only about 30% of normal, may be even less with aortocaval compression.
q_0867.trap: (D) and (E) alter parameters that do not change: the rate stays 100 to 120/min, the depth at least 5 cm and no more than 6 cm, the ratio 30 compressions to 2 breaths, and 1 breath every 6 seconds.

q_0868.stem: According to the Emergency Treatment box, how should a pregnant woman be positioned for chest compressions, and how often is the compressor role rotated?
options: On a flat, firm surface with the uterus displaced laterally by a wedge such as a rolled towel under her hip, or manually, or in a left lateral position; the compressor role is rotated every 2 minutes if possible to prevent fatigue
Sitting upright, with no rotation of the compressor
In high Fowler position, rotating every 10 minutes
Prone, rotating every 5 cycles
q_0868.rationale: The box directs positioning "on a flat, firm surface with her uterus displaced laterally with a wedge (e.g., a rolled towel placed under her hip) or manually or place her in a left lateral position," compressions at 100 to 120/min with full chest recoil, a pulse check after 5 cycles of 30 compressions and 2 breaths or about 2 minutes, and rotating the compressor role every 2 minutes.
q_0868.trap: (D) borrows the 5-cycle interval, which is when the pulse is checked, and attaches it to compressor rotation — two different timings that happen to be about the same length.

q_0869.stem: A woman at 32 weeks is choking and cannot speak or cough. What maneuver should be used?
options: Abdominal thrusts, as for any adult
Chest thrusts: standing behind her with arms under her armpits encircling her chest, pressing backward with quick thrusts until the foreign body is expelled
Back blows only
Immediate cricothyrotomy
q_0869.rationale: "Clearing an airway obstruction is usually accomplished by performing abdominal thrusts. However, during the second and third trimesters of pregnancy, chest thrusts rather than abdominal thrusts should be used." The Emergency Treatment box describes standing behind her, arms under the armpits encircling the chest, with the thumb side of the clenched fist against the middle of the sternum and the other hand over the fist.
q_0869.trap: (A) is correct for a nonpregnant adult or a woman in the first trimester, and it is the default that has to be overridden once the uterus occupies the abdomen. If she becomes unconscious, she is supported carefully to the ground, emergency services activated, and CPR begun.

q_0870.topic: the insulin requirement curve in pregnancy
q_0870.stem: A woman with type 1 diabetes at 8 weeks of gestation reports frequent hypoglycemia, especially during sleep. How should this be interpreted?
options: As an error in her technique requiring retraining
As the expected first-trimester pattern, in which maternal glucose is normally reduced and the insulin response enhanced, so the dose should be reduced by 10% to 25% at weeks 6 to 10
As early diabetic ketoacidosis
As a sign that she should stop insulin entirely
q_0870.rationale: In the first trimester "maternal blood glucose levels are normally reduced and the insulin response to glucose is enhanced," so "the insulin dose for the woman with well-controlled diabetes may have to be reduced to prevent hypoglycemia." Specifically: "in the first trimester, from weeks 6 to 10 of gestation, the insulin dose should be reduced by 10% to 25% to avoid hypoglycemia." Early hypoglycemia "occurs frequently, often during sleep."
q_0870.trap: (A) treats a physiologic shift as a teaching failure, and it is the response that leaves the dose unchanged. Nausea, vomiting, and food cravings add dietary fluctuations on top of the hormonal change.

q_0871.topic: the insulin requirement curve in pregnancy
q_0871.stem: What happens to insulin requirements after the first trimester, and when do they peak?
options: Insulin resistance begins as early as 14 to 16 weeks and continues to increase, with requirements peaking at 36 weeks and decreasing significantly after that
Requirements continue to fall through the third trimester
Requirements stay constant after 20 weeks
Requirements peak at 24 weeks and then fall steadily
q_0871.rationale: "Because insulin requirements steadily increase after the first trimester, the insulin dose must be adjusted accordingly to prevent hyperglycemia. Insulin resistance begins as early as 14 to 16 weeks of gestation and continues to increase until it stabilizes during the last few weeks of pregnancy." And: "insulin requirements normally peak at 36 weeks of gestation and decrease significantly after that."
q_0871.trap: (B) carries the first-trimester direction forward, which is the error that produces third-trimester hyperglycemia in a woman whose dose was never raised.

q_0872.topic: the insulin requirement curve in pregnancy
q_0872.stem: A woman with type 1 diabetes gave birth 6 hours ago and is eating a regular diet. What insulin dose should the nurse expect?
options: Her full pregnancy dose, to prevent rebound hyperglycemia
One-third to one-half of her most recent pregnancy dose, because the placental hormones that created the insulin resistance are gone
Double her prepregnancy dose
No insulin for the first week
q_0872.rationale: "During the first 24 hours postpartum, insulin requirements decrease substantially because the major sources of insulin resistance, the placental hormones, are greatly reduced," and "women with preexisting diabetes usually require only one-third to one-half of their most recent pregnancy insulin dose on the first postpartum day." A subcutaneous dose should be given at least 1 hour before discontinuing an IV insulin infusion.
q_0872.trap: (A) is the clinically dangerous half of this curve, because continuing the pregnancy dose after the placenta is delivered produces severe hypoglycemia.

q_0873.topic: the insulin requirement curve in pregnancy
q_0873.stem: A breastfeeding woman with type 1 diabetes checks her glucose before a late-night feeding and it is 88 mg/dL. What should she do?
options: Take her usual insulin dose and feed the baby
Consume 15 g of carbohydrates without taking insulin, since insulin requirements decrease during lactation and hypoglycemia risk is highest after late-night feedings
Skip the feeding and pump instead
Wait until the glucose falls below 70 mg/dL before acting
q_0873.rationale: "Insulin requirements in breastfeeding women decrease because of the carbohydrate used in human milk production," and they "are at increased risk for hypoglycemia after breastfeeding, particularly after late-night feeding sessions. Women should check their blood glucose level just before breastfeeding. If it is less than 100 mg/dL, they should consume 15 g of carbohydrates ... without taking insulin."
q_0873.trap: (D) waits for the treatment threshold when this is a prevention threshold. The chapter also notes that frequent hypoglycemia can reduce milk production, and that the lactation dose must be recalculated at weaning.

q_0874.stem: Which statements distinguish type 1 from type 2 diabetes as the chapter defines them? Select all that apply.
options: Type 1 accounts for 5% to 10% of cases and is caused primarily by pancreatic islet beta-cell destruction, with absolute insulin deficiency
Type 2 accounts for 90% to 95% of cases and involves insulin resistance with usually relative rather than absolute insulin deficiency
Type 1 is prone to ketoacidosis
Type 2 often goes undiagnosed for years because hyperglycemia develops gradually
Type 2 usually has an abrupt onset at a young age
q_0874.rationale: The chapter gives type 1 at 5% to 10% of all diabetes from beta-cell destruction with a tendency to ketoacidosis and an abrupt onset at a young age, and type 2 at 90% to 95% with insulin resistance and relative insulin deficiency, often undiagnosed for years because hyperglycemia develops gradually and is "often not severe enough for the person to recognize the classic signs of polyuria, polydipsia, and polyphagia."
q_0874.trap: (E) assigns type 1's onset pattern to type 2, which is what makes a gradually developing case easy to miss.

q_0875.stem: How does the chapter define gestational diabetes mellitus, and what does the definition exclude?
options: Carbohydrate intolerance that develops during pregnancy, identified during the second or third trimester, excluding women with preexisting type 1 or type 2 diabetes diagnosed during pregnancy
Any elevated glucose value at any point in pregnancy
Diabetes diagnosed at any time that resolves after birth
Insulin resistance present before conception
q_0875.rationale: "Gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM) is defined as carbohydrate intolerance that develops during pregnancy," and "it also requires that carbohydrate intolerance be identified during the second or third trimester of pregnancy." The ADA definition "excludes women with preexisting diabetes (type 1 or type 2) that is diagnosed during pregnancy" — GDM is "simply diabetes diagnosed during pregnancy that is clearly not overt (preexisting) diabetes."
q_0875.trap: (B) drops the timing clause, and the timing is what separates a woman whose fetus was exposed during organogenesis from one whose fetus was not.

q_0876.stem: A woman with no diabetes before pregnancy has two abnormal values on her oral glucose tolerance test, and her glucose is controlled by diet alone. Which White's class applies, and what would change it?
options: Class A1; requiring insulin or an oral hypoglycemic medication would make her class A2
Class A2; adding diet control would make her A1
Class B, based on her age at onset
Class F, if she develops proteinuria
q_0876.rationale: White's class A1 is a woman with "two or more abnormal values on OGTT, but fasting and postprandial glucose values are diet controlled," while class A2 is a woman "not known to have diabetes before pregnancy but requires either insulin or oral hypoglycemic medication for blood glucose control."
q_0876.trap: (C) reaches into the pregestational classes. Classes B, C, and D grade by age at onset and duration of illness, while F, R, and T name which organ has failed — nephropathy, retinitis proliferans, and renal transplant. Pregestational women fall into classes B through T.

q_0877.stem: A pregnant woman with type 1 diabetes is pale, clammy, irritable, and shaky, with shallow respirations and a rapid pulse. Her urine is negative for sugar and acetone. What is occurring?
options: Diabetic ketoacidosis
Hypoglycemia, or insulin shock
Normal pregnancy fatigue
Thyroid storm
q_0877.rationale: Table 29.2 gives hypoglycemia a rapid onset with irritability, hunger, sweating, nervousness, weakness, blurred vision, pallor, clammy skin, shallow respirations, and a rapid pulse, with urine negative for sugar and acetone and a blood glucose under 70 mg/dL.
q_0877.trap: (A) shares one symptom — headache appears in both columns — but nothing else. The cue that survives a blank moment is cold and clammy versus hot and dry: ketoacidosis brings flushed dry skin, rapid breathing, and a fruity acetone breath odor, with urine positive for sugar and acetone.

q_0878.stem: A pregnant woman with type 1 diabetes has a blood glucose of 240 mg/dL with nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, and fruity breath. A colleague says the glucose is not high enough for ketoacidosis. How should the nurse respond?
options: Agree, since DKA requires a glucose above 300 mg/dL
Disagree: in pregnancy, DKA may occur with blood glucose levels barely exceeding 200 mg/dL, compared with 300 to 350 mg/dL in the nonpregnant state
Agree, but recheck in 2 hours
Disagree, because DKA is diagnosed by glucose alone
q_0878.rationale: "DKA may occur with blood glucose levels barely exceeding 200 mg/dL compared with 300 to 350 mg/dL in the nonpregnant state." It occurs most often in the second and third trimesters, "when the diabetogenic effect of pregnancy is greatest," and "DKA is a medical emergency ... Ketoacidosis occurring at any time during pregnancy can lead to intrauterine fetal death."
q_0878.trap: (A) applies the nonpregnant threshold, which is precisely the delay this fact exists to prevent.

q_0879.stem: A woman with type 1 diabetes in preterm labor is receiving terbutaline and has been given betamethasone. What complication should the nurse anticipate?
options: Hypoglycemia from increased glucose uptake
Diabetic ketoacidosis, because beta-mimetic drugs for tocolysis and corticosteroids for fetal lung maturity can precipitate hyperglycemia and DKA
Thyroid storm
No metabolic effect from either drug
q_0879.rationale: The chapter names among DKA triggers "beta-mimetic drugs such as terbutaline (Brethine) for tocolysis ... or corticosteroids given to enhance fetal lung maturation," alongside illness or infection and poor adherence to treatment.
q_0879.trap: (A) reverses the direction of both drugs' metabolic effects. Both are given for good obstetric reasons, which is what makes the interaction worth anticipating rather than avoiding.

q_0880.stem: A pregnant woman's blood glucose is 62 mg/dL and she is alert. What does Table 29.2 direct?
options: Consume 2 to 4 glucose tablets or gel, 8 to 16 g of carbohydrate, immediately, and recheck the blood glucose in 15 minutes
Give 50% dextrose IV push
Administer 1 mg of glucagon intramuscularly
Give a full meal and recheck in 1 hour
q_0880.rationale: "If blood glucose is <70 mg/dL, consume 2–4 glucose tablets or gel (8–16 g carbohydrate) immediately," then "recheck blood glucose level in 15 min." If still under 70, repeat, recheck again in 15 minutes, and if still low "notify health care provider immediately."
q_0880.trap: (B) and (C) are the interventions for an unconscious woman, where oral glucose would be an aspiration risk. The parenteral options are 50% dextrose IV push, 5% to 10% dextrose IV drip, or 1 mg glucagon intramuscularly.

q_0881.topic: maternal and fetal risks of diabetes
q_0881.stem: A woman with pregestational diabetes is carrying a fetus with an estimated weight of 4300 g. Why is the risk of shoulder dystocia greater than for another macrosomic infant of the same weight?
options: Because infants of women with diabetes tend to have a disproportionate increase in shoulder, trunk, and chest size
Because the maternal pelvis is smaller in diabetes
Because diabetic pregnancies are always postterm
There is no difference in risk at the same weight
q_0881.rationale: "Infants born to women with diabetes tend to have a disproportionate increase in shoulder, trunk, and chest size. Because of this tendency, the risk for shoulder dystocia is greater in these infants than in other macrosomic infants." Macrosomia occurs in approximately 40% of pregestational diabetic pregnancies and up to 50% of pregnancies complicated by GDM.
q_0881.trap: (D) treats weight as the whole story. The asymmetry between head and shoulders, not the number on the scale, is what makes the birth difficult.

q_0882.topic: maternal and fetal risks of diabetes
q_0882.stem: What is the mechanism by which maternal hyperglycemia produces a macrosomic fetus?
options: Maternal insulin crosses the placenta and acts as a growth hormone

The fetal pancreas begins secreting insulin at 10 to 14 weeks and responds to maternal hyperglycemia with hyperinsulinism; insulin acts as a growth hormone, producing excess glycogen, protein, and adipose tissue
Excess maternal glucose is stored directly as fetal fat without fetal insulin
Placental hormones directly stimulate fetal growth
q_0882.rationale: "The fetal pancreas begins to secrete insulin at 10 to 14 weeks of gestation. The fetus responds to maternal hyperglycemia by secreting large amounts of insulin (hyperinsulinism). Insulin acts as a growth hormone, causing the fetus to produce excess stores of glycogen, protein, and adipose tissue and leading to increased fetal size, or macrosomia."
q_0882.trap: (A) has maternal insulin crossing the placenta, which it does not — the fetus makes its own, and that is also why the newborn becomes hypoglycemic when the maternal glucose supply stops at birth.

q_0883.topic: maternal and fetal risks of diabetes
q_0883.stem: A woman diagnosed with gestational diabetes at 26 weeks asks whether her baby is at risk for birth defects. What does the chapter support?
options: That no increase in birth defects has been found among infants of women who develop GDM after the first trimester, because the critical period of organ formation has already passed
That cardiac and neural tube defects are equally likely as in pregestational diabetes
That the risk is higher than in pregestational diabetes
That all diabetic pregnancies carry the same anomaly risk regardless of timing
q_0883.rationale: "No increase in the incidence of birth defects has been found among infants of women who develop GDM after the first trimester because the critical period of organ formation has already passed." In pregestational diabetes, by contrast, "hyperglycemia during the first trimester of pregnancy, when organs and organ systems are forming, is the main cause of diabetes-associated birth defects," affecting primarily the cardiovascular system and the CNS.
q_0883.trap: (B) applies the pregestational risk to a woman whose hyperglycemia began after organogenesis. Both groups still face macrosomia and neonatal hypoglycemia, which come from later fetal hyperinsulinism.

q_0884.topic: maternal and fetal risks of diabetes
q_0884.stem: Why does the chapter treat infection as more than a local problem in a pregnant woman with diabetes?
options: Because infection causes increased insulin resistance and may result in ketoacidosis
Because antibiotics are contraindicated in diabetic pregnancy
Because infection lowers blood glucose dangerously
Because infection only affects the urinary tract in these women
q_0884.rationale: "Infections are more common and more serious in pregnant women with diabetes," because carbohydrate metabolism disorders alter resistance to infection — "the inflammatory response, leukocyte function, and vaginal pH are all affected." And: "Infection is serious because it causes increased insulin resistance and may result in ketoacidosis."
q_0884.trap: (C) reverses the metabolic direction, which would make a nurse watch for the wrong complication entirely.

q_0885.stem: Which target plasma glucose values does Table 29.3 give for pregnancy? Select all that apply.
options: Before breakfast, 60 to less than 95 mg/dL
Before lunch or dinner, 60 to 105 mg/dL
One hour after a meal, less than 140 mg/dL
Two hours after a meal, less than 120 mg/dL
Two a.m. to 6 a.m., less than 60 mg/dL
q_0885.rationale: Table 29.3 gives before breakfast 60 to under 95, before lunch or dinner 60 to 105, 1-hour postmeal under 140, 2-hour postmeal under 120, and 2 a.m. to 6 a.m. greater than 60.
q_0885.trap: (E) inverts the overnight target. The overnight value has a floor rather than a ceiling, because the danger in those hours is hypoglycemia during sleep.

q_0886.stem: A woman with diabetes asks whether she should test her urine to guide her diet. What does the chapter direct, and what is the hemoglobin A1c caution?
options: Dietary management must be based on blood, not urine, glucose levels; and iron deficiency anemia falsely increases the A1c level
Urine glucose testing is the basis of dietary management; A1c is unaffected by anemia
Both are equally valid; A1c reflects 3 months of control in pregnancy
Neither blood nor urine testing is needed if she follows her diet
q_0886.rationale: "Dietary management during diabetic pregnancy must be based on blood (not urine) glucose levels." The Nursing Alert states: "Iron deficiency anemia falsely increases the A1c level." Because red cells turn over more rapidly in pregnancy, the A1c reflects "only the previous 2 to 6 weeks," and levels under 6% to 6.5% in early pregnancy are associated with the lowest rates of adverse fetal outcomes.
q_0886.trap: (C) carries the nonpregnant 3-month window into pregnancy, which would make a nurse over-read a single result.

q_0887.stem: Which dietary instructions match the chapter's teaching for a pregnant woman with diabetes? Select all that apply.
options: Divide daily food intake among three meals and two or three snacks
Eat a substantial bedtime snack of at least 25 g of complex carbohydrate with some protein or fat
Never go more than 4 hours without food intake
Eat consistently each day and never skip meals or snacks
Restrict all carbohydrates to avoid postmeal spikes
q_0887.rationale: Intake is "best distributed among three meals and three snacks," with a bedtime snack of "at least 25 g of complex carbohydrate with some protein or fat ... to help prevent hypoglycemia and starvation ketosis during the night." "Going more than 4 hours without food intake increases the risk for episodes of hypoglycemia," and the teaching box directs eating consistently and never skipping meals or snacks.
q_0887.trap: (E) contradicts the prescribed macronutrient distribution of 33% to 40% carbohydrates, and complex carbohydrates are specifically chosen because "the starch and protein in such foods help to regulate the blood glucose level by producing a more gradual release of glucose."

q_0888.stem: A woman with diabetes plans to walk after dinner. Her glucose is 210 mg/dL and her urine is positive for ketones. What should the nurse advise?
options: Walk as planned, since exercise will lower the glucose
Avoid exercise, because hyperglycemia and ketosis can worsen with physical activity
Walk after taking 15 to 30 g of carbohydrates
Walk twice as long to clear the ketones
q_0888.rationale: "Women should avoid exercise if they have positive urine ketones or a blood glucose greater than 200 mg/dL because hyperglycemia and ketosis can worsen with physical activity." The other numeric rule runs the opposite way: "if the blood glucose is less than 100 mg/dL, women should consume 15 to 30 g of carbohydrates to prevent hypoglycemia."
q_0888.trap: (A) applies ordinary diabetes teaching — activity lowers glucose — to the one situation where the chapter forbids it. (C) applies the low-glucose rule to a high-glucose reading.

q_0889.stem: A woman is prescribed lispro insulin. When should it be given, and what is its onset?
options: Immediately before mealtime, with an onset of about 15 minutes
Thirty minutes before meals, with an onset of 2 hours
At bedtime, with no peak
Twice daily regardless of meals, with a peak at 6 to 12 hours
q_0889.rationale: Table 29.4 gives lispro and aspart an onset of 15 minutes, and the chapter notes that these rapid-acting analogues "are convenient to use because they are injected immediately before mealtime." Because their effects last only 3 to 5 hours, "most clients require a longer-acting insulin in addition."
q_0889.trap: (D) describes intermediate-acting NPH, whose 6- to 12-hour peak is when an unexpected drop occurs. Matching the action time to the meal is what prevents hypoglycemia from a delayed or missed meal.

q_0890.stem: A woman takes glargine insulin. Which statements are accurate? Select all that apply.
options: It is a long-acting analogue with no pronounced peak and a 24-hour duration
It is usually administered at bedtime
It cannot be mixed with any other insulin in the same syringe
Prepared syringes are stable for 2 weeks in the refrigerator
It may be combined with rapid-acting insulin in one syringe to reduce injections
q_0890.rationale: Glargine and detemir "are long-acting insulin analogues ... released slowly, with no pronounced peak," both appear safe in pregnancy, and Box 29.1 states that "glargine insulin is usually administered at bedtime. It cannot be mixed with any other insulin in the same syringe. Prepared syringes are stable for 2 weeks in the refrigerator."
q_0890.trap: (E) is attractive because glargine and a rapid-acting insulin are often given together — as separate injections. The box's rule is explicit.

q_0891.stem: A woman is drawing up NPH and rapid-acting insulin in one syringe. What is the correct sequence?
options: Inject air into the NPH vial, inject air into the rapid-acting vial, withdraw the rapid-acting dose, then withdraw the NPH dose without adding more air to the NPH vial
Inject air into the rapid-acting vial first, then withdraw NPH first
Withdraw NPH first, then rapid-acting
Draw each into a separate syringe, since they cannot be mixed
q_0891.rationale: The teaching box gives the order: air into the NPH vial first, then air into the rapid-acting vial, then withdraw the rapid-acting dose, then "without adding more air to the NPH vial, carefully withdraw NPH dose." Box 29.1 confirms that regular insulin can be mixed with NPH in the same syringe, as can lispro.
q_0891.trap: (C) is the most common reversal and would contaminate the clear insulin with the cloudy one. If a mixed syringe is stored for later use, it should be rotated 20 times before injection.

q_0892.stem: Which statements about insulin injection sites and storage match Box 29.1? Select all that apply.
options: The abdomen is the preferred site because insulin is best absorbed there
Other sites include the upper outer arm — not the deltoid area — the thighs, and the buttocks
Each injection should be given 2 inches from the previous injection in one quadrant before moving to another quadrant
Unopened vials are refrigerated until their expiration date and are never frozen, while a vial in use may be kept at room temperature for up to 1 month
Premixed insulins are preferred in pregnancy for convenience
q_0892.rationale: Box 29.1 gives the abdomen as preferred, the upper outer arm excluding the deltoid, thighs, and buttocks as alternatives, 2 inches between injections within a quadrant, and the storage rules for unopened and in-use vials.
q_0892.trap: (E) reverses the chapter's position: premixed insulins "usually are not in the correct percentages to be effective in pregnancy. Therefore they are rarely used."

q_0893.stem: A woman with severe obesity, a strong family history of type 2 diabetes, and GDM in a previous pregnancy presents for her first prenatal visit at 10 weeks. When should she be screened?
options: At 24 to 28 weeks, like all other women
At the initial prenatal visit, by one of the methods used to diagnose diabetes in the nonpregnant population, and rescreened at 24 to 28 weeks if that result is negative
Only if she develops glycosuria
At 36 weeks
q_0893.rationale: "Although most women are screened for GDM between 24 and 28 weeks of gestation, women with strong risk factors should be screened earlier in pregnancy" — those with "severe obesity, a strong family history of type 2 diabetes, and a history of GDM in a previous pregnancy" are tested at the initial visit using nonpregnant diagnostic methods, and "if negative, they should be rescreened at 24 to 28 weeks of gestation for GDM."
q_0893.trap: (C) waits for a sign that arrives late or not at all, and "more than half of all women diagnosed with GDM do not have these risk factors" — which is why screening is universal rather than risk-based.

q_0894.stem: A woman is given a 50-g oral glucose load without fasting and has a 1-hour plasma glucose of 152 mg/dL. What happens next?
options: She is diagnosed with GDM
This is a positive screen in the two-step method, so she returns on another day for a 3-hour 100-g oral glucose tolerance test, and GDM is diagnosed if two or more values are met or exceeded
The test is repeated fasting
No further testing is needed if she has no risk factors
q_0894.rationale: The two-step approach begins with "a 50-g oral glucose load followed by a plasma glucose measurement 1 hour later. The woman need not be fasting. A glucose value of 130 to 140 mg/dL or higher is considered a positive screen," followed by "a 3-hour (100-g) oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT) on another day." GDM is diagnosed "if two or more values are met or exceeded."
q_0894.trap: (A) treats a screen as a diagnosis. Approximately 95% of United States obstetricians continue to use the two-step approach.

q_0895.stem: How does the one-step method differ from the two-step method?
options: It uses a 75-g OGTT between 24 and 28 weeks and diagnoses GDM if only one glucose value is exceeded, significantly increasing the incidence of GDM — likely double that found with the two-step method
It uses a 100-g load and requires two abnormal values
It is a nonfasting screen only
It is performed only in the first trimester
q_0895.rationale: The one-step method is "a 75-g OGTT diagnostic test ... between 24 and 28 weeks" with fasting, 1-hour, and 2-hour draws, and "a diagnosis of GDM is made if only one glucose value is exceeded." It "significantly increases the incidence of GDM, likely double that found using the two-step method." ACOG keeps the two-step method because there is no evidence the one-step method improves outcomes while it does increase costs.
q_0895.trap: (B) swaps the two methods' glucose loads and diagnostic rules. The cue is to count the values needed: two for the two-step, one for the one-step.

q_0896.stem: How should a woman prepare for an oral glucose tolerance test?
options: After an overnight fast and at least 3 days of unrestricted diet with at least 150 g of carbohydrates and normal physical activity, avoiding caffeine and abstaining from smoking for 12 hours beforehand
After fasting for 24 hours
After 3 days of carbohydrate restriction
With no special preparation
q_0896.rationale: The OGTT is "administered after an overnight fast and at least 3 days of unrestricted diet (at least 150 g of carbohydrates) and physical activity. The woman is instructed to avoid caffeine because it increases glucose levels and to abstain from smoking for 12 hours before the test."
q_0896.trap: (C) is the intuitive preparation — cut carbohydrates before a glucose test — and it invalidates the result, because the test measures how she handles a normal intake.

q_0897.stem: A woman with GDM has fasting glucose values persistently above 95 mg/dL despite diet and exercise. What happens next, and which medication is preferred?
options: Pharmacologic therapy is begun, and insulin is the preferred medication recommended by the ADA
Diet therapy is intensified for another month before any medication
Glyburide is started first because it is least likely to cross the placenta
No treatment is needed unless postmeal values are also elevated
q_0897.rationale: "If fasting plasma glucose levels are persistently greater than 95 mg/dL, 1-hour postmeal levels are persistently greater than 140 mg/dL, or 2-hour postmeal levels are persistently greater than 120 mg/dL despite nutritional therapy and exercise, pharmacologic therapy is begun," and "insulin is recommended by the ADA as the preferred medication for women with GDM." About one-third of women with GDM require medication.
q_0897.trap: (C) inverts the placental transfer comparison and the recommendation. Metformin "readily crosses the placenta in levels as high as maternal levels," glyburide crosses "in smaller amounts," and yet "current recommendations suggest the use of metformin over glyburide" — while insulin remains preferred because the oral agents cross the placenta and lack long-term neonatal safety data.

q_0898.stem: A woman with GDM has excellent diet-controlled glucose levels, normal fetal growth, no hypertension, and no prior stillbirth. What antepartum fetal testing does the chapter recommend?
options: Twice-weekly nonstress tests beginning at 32 weeks
Routine antepartum fetal testing is not performed, because these women are at low risk for intrauterine fetal death, unless she also has hypertension, a prior stillbirth, or suspected macrosomia
Weekly biophysical profiles from 28 weeks
Daily kick counts and nothing else, throughout pregnancy
q_0898.rationale: "Women with GDM whose blood glucose levels are well controlled by diet are at low risk for IUFD. Therefore antepartum fetal testing is not performed routinely in these women unless they also have hypertension, a history of a prior stillbirth, or suspected macrosomia."
q_0898.trap: (A) is the schedule for women with those complications or on medication, and applying it to every GDM patient over-treats a low-risk group.

q_0899.stem: During labor for a woman with GDM, what glucose range is targeted and why, and how is it usually achieved?
options: 80 to 110 mg/dL, because levels in this range decrease the incidence of neonatal hypoglycemia; excellent control is usually possible by avoiding IV fluids containing dextrose
140 to 180 mg/dL, to provide energy for labor
Below 60 mg/dL, to prevent fetal hyperinsulinism
Any level, since labor is too short to matter
q_0899.rationale: In GDM, "blood glucose levels are monitored every 1 to 2 hours to maintain levels between 80 and 110 mg/dL. Levels within this range decrease the incidence of neonatal hypoglycemia," and "it is usually possible to maintain excellent glucose control in women with GDM during labor by avoiding the use of IV fluids containing dextrose."
q_0899.trap: (B) borrows the rationale that applies to pregestational diabetes, where a dextrose-containing solution is piggybacked once active labor begins or glucose falls below 70 — a different plan for a different metabolic starting point.

q_0900.stem: What postpartum follow-up does the chapter recommend after a pregnancy complicated by GDM?
options: A 75-g 2-hour OGTT or fasting plasma glucose at 6 to 12 weeks postpartum, then lifelong repeat screening at least every 3 years
No follow-up, since GDM resolves at birth
A single fasting glucose at the 6-week visit and nothing further
Annual A1c testing beginning at age 45
q_0900.rationale: ACOG recommends "assessing all women who had GDM for carbohydrate intolerance with a 75-g, 2-hour OGTT or a fasting plasma glucose level at 6 to 12 weeks postpartum," then "lifelong repeat screening at least every 3 years." Up to one-third are found to have diabetes or impaired glucose metabolism at that screening, and the chance of developing type 2 diabetes within 10 to 20 years is as high as 70%.
q_0900.trap: (B) treats resolution of the pregnancy as resolution of the risk. The chapter's counterweight is that "progression to type 2 diabetes is not inevitable" for women who exercise, become less sedentary, and eat a healthy diet.

q_0901.topic: intrapartum and postpartum care in pregestational diabetes
q_0901.stem: A woman with pregestational diabetes is in active labor. How often is her glucose checked, what is the target, and why?
options: Hourly, with short-acting insulin titrated to keep the level under 110 mg/dL, because hyperglycemia during labor can cause metabolic problems in the neonate, particularly hypoglycemia
Every 4 hours, with a target of 140 mg/dL
Once on admission, since labor is brief
Hourly, with a target above 140 mg/dL to fuel labor
q_0901.rationale: "During active labor, blood glucose levels should be checked hourly," with short-acting insulin titrated to maintain levels "less than 110 mg/dL," because "hyperglycemia during labor can cause metabolic problems in the neonate, particularly hypoglycemia." The infusion is normal saline or lactated Ringer's initially, with 5% dextrose piggybacked once active labor begins or glucose falls below 70 mg/dL.
q_0901.trap: (D) confuses the woman's energy needs with her glucose target. The dextrose infusion supplies the calories; the insulin keeps the level down.

q_0902.topic: intrapartum and postpartum care in pregestational diabetes
q_0902.stem: A woman with pregestational diabetes has a cesarean birth scheduled. What does the chapter direct about timing and insulin?
options: Schedule it in the early morning to facilitate glycemic control; she takes her full dose of insulin the night before, no morning insulin is given on the day of surgery, and she has nothing by mouth after midnight
Schedule it in the afternoon and give her usual morning insulin
Hold the evening insulin and give the morning dose
Give a double dose the night before to cover the fasting period
q_0902.rationale: A scheduled cesarean "should be scheduled in the early morning to facilitate glycemic control. Women should take their full dose of insulin the night before surgery. No morning insulin is given on the day of surgery," and she is given nothing by mouth after midnight. Regional anesthesia "is recommended because hypoglycemia can be detected earlier if the woman is awake."
q_0902.trap: (B) gives insulin to a fasting woman, which is the combination that produces intraoperative hypoglycemia.

q_0903.topic: intrapartum and postpartum care in pregestational diabetes
q_0903.stem: Which postpartum complications are more likely in a woman with pregestational diabetes? Select all that apply.
options: Preeclampsia or eclampsia
Hemorrhage, particularly if the uterus was overdistended by hydramnios or a macrosomic fetus, or overstimulated by oxytocin induction
Infection such as endometritis
Mastitis if she breastfeeds
Hypertension caused by the fall in insulin requirements
q_0903.rationale: The chapter names preeclampsia or eclampsia, hemorrhage, and infection, with hemorrhage tied to a uterus "overdistended (hydramnios, macrosomic fetus) or overstimulated (oxytocin induction)" and endometritis more likely. Breastfeeding mothers with diabetes are also "at increased risk for mastitis," and poor metabolic control "may delay lactogenesis and contribute to decreased milk production."
q_0903.trap: (E) invents a hemodynamic consequence for a metabolic change. The fall in insulin requirement causes hypoglycemia if the dose is not reduced, not hypertension.

q_0904.topic: intrapartum and postpartum care in pregestational diabetes
q_0904.stem: Which contraceptive approach does the chapter describe as often recommended for a woman with diabetes, and what is said about the transdermal patch?
options: Long-acting reversible contraception, an IUD or implant, which does not appear to affect glycemic control postpartum; the transdermal patch is contraindicated in obese women, with a higher failure rate above 90 kg
Combined oral contraceptives for all women with diabetes; the patch is preferred in obesity
Barrier methods only, because hormones are contraindicated
Sterilization for every woman with diabetes after one birth
q_0904.rationale: LARC is "considered quite effective and is often recommended. These forms of contraception do not appear to affect glycemic control postpartum." The transdermal patch is "contraindicated in obese women," with a higher failure rate above 90 kg and possible increased thromboembolic risk. Combined oral contraceptives are controversial and may be prescribed to nonsmoking women without vascular disease, while progestin-only pills may be used by women with vascular disease.
q_0904.trap: (D) generalizes a recommendation the chapter reserves for a woman "who has completed her family, or who has significant vascular disease or other end-organ complications" — and it notes that vasectomy for the partner is safer than surgical sterilization in a woman with diabetes.

q_0905.stem: Which findings distinguish hyperemesis gravidarum from ordinary nausea and vomiting of pregnancy?
options: Weight loss, electrolyte imbalance, nutritional deficiencies, and ketonuria
The number of emesis episodes per day
Onset before 10 weeks of gestation
Nausea that persists past 12 weeks
q_0905.rationale: "When vomiting during pregnancy becomes excessive enough to cause weight loss, electrolyte imbalance, nutritional deficiencies, and ketonuria, the disorder is termed hyperemesis gravidarum." Ordinary nausea and vomiting complicates 50% to 80% of pregnancies, typically begins at 4 to 10 weeks, and is "typically benign, with no significant metabolic alterations or risks to the mother or fetus."
q_0905.trap: (B) counts episodes instead of consequences, which is how a woman with frequent but tolerated vomiting gets over-treated and a woman with fewer episodes and ketonuria gets missed.

q_0906.stem: What does the chapter identify as the most important initial laboratory test in suspected hyperemesis gravidarum, and what other test is often added?
options: A determination of ketonuria; and because of the recognized association between hyperemesis and hyperthyroidism, thyroid levels may also be measured
A complete blood count; and a fasting glucose
Liver function tests; and a urine culture
Serum hCG; and a coagulation panel
q_0906.rationale: "The most important initial laboratory test to be obtained is a determination of ketonuria," and "because of the recognized association between hyperemesis gravidarum and hyperthyroidism, thyroid levels may also be measured." Other tests help rule out gastroenteritis, pyelonephritis, pancreatitis, cholecystitis, peptic ulcer, and hepatitis.
q_0906.trap: (D) reaches for a hormone that is a proposed cause rather than a diagnostic test, and it misses the thyroid link that can change the treatment entirely.

q_0907.stem: A woman with nausea and vomiting of pregnancy has not responded to dietary measures. What does the chapter give as initial medical management?
options: Pyridoxine, vitamin B6, either alone or in combination with doxylamine
Ondansetron, because it is best studied in pregnancy
A corticosteroid taper
Promethazine as first-line therapy
q_0907.rationale: The chapter names "pyridoxine (vitamin B6), either alone or in combination with doxylamine (Unisom) as initial medical management." Diclegis is the single-tablet delayed-release combination, with cost as its disadvantage, and Bonjesta is a second extended-release brand.
q_0907.trap: (B) names the drug most familiar from practice, and the chapter says its "use in pregnancy has not been well studied." Dopamine antagonists such as promethazine "have been found to be effective, but their safety in pregnancy has not been proven," and corticosteroids are reserved for nonresponders and "avoided if possible during the first trimester" because of a possible facial clefting risk.

q_0908.stem: A woman hospitalized with hyperemesis has stopped vomiting. How should feedings resume, and what does the chapter emphasize about her care?
options: Small amounts at frequent intervals — limited oral fluids and bland foods such as crackers, toast, or baked chicken — with intake and output including emesis measured accurately, and calm, compassionate care in a quiet, odor-free environment
A full regular diet immediately to restore nutrition
Nothing by mouth for another 48 hours
High-fat foods to replace lost calories
q_0908.rationale: "Once the vomiting has stopped, feedings are started in small amounts at frequent intervals" — "limited amounts of oral fluids and bland foods such as crackers, toast, or baked chicken." Intake and output including the amount of emesis are measured accurately, and the woman "needs calm, compassionate, and sympathetic care," with irritability, tearfulness, and mood changes recognized as consistent with the disorder.
q_0908.trap: (D) is the opposite of the dietary teaching, which calls for "dry, bland, low-fat, and high-protein foods," with cold foods often better tolerated than warm.

q_0909.stem: Which instructions appear in the Teaching for Self-Management box on diet for hyperemesis gravidarum? Select all that apply.
options: Avoid an empty stomach; eat at least every 2 to 3 hours, separating liquids from solids and alternating every 2 to 3 hours
Eat a high-protein snack at bedtime
In general, eat what sounds good rather than trying to balance meals, following the salty and sweet approach
Eat protein after sweets, and try ginger tea or warm ginger ale made with sugar rather than artificial sweetener
Maintain a strictly balanced diet at every meal to protect the fetus
q_0909.rationale: The box lists avoiding an empty stomach with frequent small intake and separated liquids and solids, a high-protein bedtime snack, eating what sounds good rather than balancing meals, the salty and sweet approach with junk foods permitted, protein after sweets, dairy products, a Popsicle for vomiting on an empty stomach, ginger tea, warm ginger ale with sugar, water with lemon, and drinking from a cup with a lid.
q_0909.trap: (E) is the instinct of good prenatal nutrition teaching and is exactly what the box suspends — for this woman, getting anything down is the goal.

q_0910.stem: Which findings help distinguish hyperthyroidism from the normal changes of pregnancy?
options: Weight loss, goiter, and a pulse rate greater than 100 beats/min, with elevated T3 and T4 and greatly suppressed TSH
Heat intolerance and fatigue alone
Weight gain and cold intolerance
Nausea and anxiety alone
q_0910.rationale: Hyperthyroidism presents with heat intolerance, diaphoresis, fatigue, anxiety, emotional lability, and tachycardia, but the three findings that separate it from normal pregnancy are "weight loss, goiter, and a pulse rate greater than 100 beats/min," with laboratory findings of "elevated T3 and T4 levels and greatly suppressed TSH levels." Graves disease causes 90% to 95% of cases in pregnancy.
q_0910.trap: (C) describes hypothyroidism, whose symptoms are weight gain, lethargy, decreased exercise capacity, and cold intolerance, with elevated TSH with or without low T4.

q_0911.stem: A woman with Graves disease is 8 weeks pregnant and taking methimazole. What does the chapter direct?
options: Continue methimazole throughout pregnancy

Use propylthiouracil in the first trimester only, because methimazole taken during the first trimester can cause choanal or esophageal atresia, facial anomalies, hearing loss, developmental delay, and congenital cardiac malformations, then switch to methimazole after the first trimester
Stop all antithyroid medication until after birth
Switch to radioactive iodine therapy
q_0911.rationale: The chapter directs that "PTU be used only in the first trimester of pregnancy," and "after the first trimester, women requiring drug therapy ... should be switched to MMI for the remainder of pregnancy," because propylthiouracil "can cause hepatic toxicity serious enough to require liver transplantation" while methimazole in the first trimester causes the listed anomalies.
q_0911.trap: (D) names the one treatment that is absolutely excluded: "radioactive iodine must not be used in diagnosis or treatment of hyperthyroidism in pregnancy because therapeutic doses given to treat maternal thyroid disease may also destroy the fetal thyroid."

q_0912.stem: A woman taking an antithyroid medication reports fever and an unexpected sore throat. What should the nurse tell her?
options: These are expected side effects requiring no action
These suggest agranulocytosis: she should report them to the health care provider and immediately stop taking the medication
She should double the dose to control her symptoms
These indicate thyroid storm
q_0912.rationale: The most common side effects of antithyroid drugs are pruritus and skin rash; the severe one is "agranulocytosis, which occurs rarely and usually develops only in older women and in those taking high doses. Symptoms ... are fever and unexpected sore throat, which should be reported to the health care provider; in addition, the woman should immediately stop taking the medication."
q_0912.trap: (D) is the other febrile emergency in this chapter, and the discriminator is the rest of the picture: thyroid storm brings restlessness, tachycardia, vomiting, or stupor in response to stress such as labor, infection, preeclampsia, or surgery.

q_0913.stem: A woman with partially treated hyperthyroidism develops fever, restlessness, tachycardia, and vomiting during labor. What is the treatment sequence?
options: IV fluids and oxygen, along with high doses of propylthiouracil, and after the PTU is administered, iodide; other medications include antipyretics, dexamethasone, and beta-blockers
Iodide first, followed by propylthiouracil
Beta-blockers alone
Methimazole and antipyretics only
q_0913.rationale: The Nursing Alert on thyroid storm directs: "Intravenous fluids and oxygen are administered, along with high doses of propylthiouracil (PTU). After administration of PTU, iodide is given. Other medications include antipyretics, dexamethasone, and beta-blockers."
q_0913.trap: (B) reverses the order the alert states explicitly, which is the detail this emergency turns on.

q_0914.stem: A woman with hypothyroidism takes levothyroxine and a prenatal iron supplement. What teaching applies, and what happens to her dose as pregnancy progresses?
options: Take levothyroxine at a different time of day, at least 4 hours apart from the iron, because ferrous sulfate decreases absorption of T4; and increased doses of thyroid hormone are usually required as pregnancy progresses
Take them together to improve adherence; the dose stays constant
Stop the iron while taking levothyroxine; the dose decreases through pregnancy
Take levothyroxine only in the third trimester
q_0914.rationale: The Medication Alert states: "If taking iron supplementation, pregnant women should be told to take levothyroxine at a different time of day, at least 4 h apart, from their iron tablets because ferrous sulfate decreases absorption of T4." The usual starting dose is 0.1 to 0.15 mg/day, adjusted by 25 to 50 mcg every 4 weeks based on maternal TSH, and "as pregnancy progresses, increased doses of thyroid hormone are usually required."
q_0914.trap: (C) solves the interaction by stopping a supplement most pregnant women need. Separating the doses in time is the fix, and levothyroxine is considered safe while breastfeeding.

q_0915.stem: A nurse is classifying risk factors for a pregnant woman. Which definition matches the biophysical category?
options: Factors that originate within the pregnant woman or fetus and affect the development or functioning of either one or both
Maternal behaviors and adverse life events that have a negative effect on health
Factors arising from the context in which the woman and family live
Hazards in the workplace and the woman's general environment
q_0915.rationale: "Biophysical risks include factors that originate within the pregnant woman or fetus and affect the development or functioning of either one or both," with examples of genetic disorders, nutritional and general health status, and medical or obstetric illnesses.
q_0915.trap: (B), (C), and (D) define the psychosocial, sociodemographic, and environmental categories respectively. The phrase "originate within" is what makes the biophysical category answerable without memorizing every example.

q_0916.stem: In which category does Box 26.1 file smoking, caffeine, alcohol, and drug use?
options: Biophysical, because they act on the body
Psychosocial, because the category covers maternal behaviors and adverse life events
Sociodemographic
Environmental
q_0916.rationale: Box 26.1 files smoking, caffeine, alcohol, drugs, and psychologic status under psychosocial factors, because "psychosocial risks consist of maternal behaviors and adverse life events that have a negative effect on the health of the pregnant woman or fetus."
q_0916.trap: (A) is the intuitive filing — these substances have physical effects — and it is the error a categorization item is built on. Biophysical is reserved for what originates within the woman or fetus, not for anything with a physical mechanism.

q_0917.stem: Which factors does Box 26.1 place in the sociodemographic category? Select all that apply.
options: Low income, which underlies many other risk factors
Lack of prenatal care, since failure to diagnose and treat complications early is a major risk factor
Age at both ends of the childbearing spectrum
Parity, marital status, and ethnicity
Genetic disorders and ABO incompatibility
q_0917.rationale: The sociodemographic factors are low income, lack of prenatal care, age, parity, marital status, social determinants of health such as rural residence, and ethnicity. Sociodemographic risks "arise from the context in which the pregnant woman and family live."
q_0917.trap: (E) is a biophysical genetic consideration, listed in Box 26.1 alongside defective genes, transmissible inherited disorders, chromosomal anomalies, multiple gestation, and large fetal size.

q_0918.stem: A woman has three separate identified risk factors, each described as minor. How should the nurse interpret this?
options: Minor risks can be disregarded individually and collectively
Risk factors are interrelated and cumulative in their effects
Only the most severe factor determines her risk
Risk is determined by counting factors, with three or more defining high risk
q_0918.rationale: The chapter states it in one sentence: "Risk factors are interrelated and cumulative in their effects." Categories exist because risk was formerly "evaluated only from a medical standpoint," and the broader grouping reflects threats to health and pregnancy outcome.
q_0918.trap: (D) turns a qualitative principle into a counting rule, which the chapter does not support — the interaction among factors, not the tally, is the point.

q_0919.stem: Which statements reflect the chapter's qualifications about age and ethnicity as risk factors? Select all that apply.
options: Women at both ends of the childbearing age spectrum have an increased incidence of poor outcomes, but age may not be a risk factor in all cases
The risks to women older than 35 are not from age alone but from considerations such as previous pregnancies, genetics, medical history, lifestyle, nutrition, and prenatal care
Although ethnicity by itself is not a major risk, race is associated with some poor pregnancy outcomes
In the United States, Black women have rates of preterm birth almost twice as high as those of other racial and ethnic groups
Advanced maternal age is an inherent biologic risk that cannot be modified by any other factor
q_0919.rationale: The chapter qualifies both factors deliberately, stating that age "may not be a risk factor in all cases," that older women's risks come from accumulated considerations rather than age alone, and that ethnicity by itself is not a major risk while race is associated with poor outcomes — with the preterm birth disparity stated numerically.
q_0919.trap: (E) contradicts the sentence immediately preceding it in the text. Older women do face more chronic hypertension, preeclampsia, diabetes, prolonged labor, cesarean birth, previa, abruption, and death — but the chapter attributes these to what accumulates with age, not to age itself.

q_0920.topic: specific pregnancy problems and risk factors
q_0920.subtopic: too much fluid and too little
q_0920.stem: Which conditions does Box 26.2 list as risk factors for polyhydramnios? Select all that apply.
options: Poorly controlled diabetes mellitus
Fetal congenital anomalies such as gastrointestinal obstruction or central nervous system abnormalities
Twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome
Fetomaternal hemorrhage and genetic disorders
Renal agenesis
q_0920.rationale: Box 26.2's polyhydramnios list is poorly controlled diabetes, fetomaternal hemorrhage, fetal congenital anomalies such as gastrointestinal obstruction or CNS abnormalities, genetic disorders, and twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome.
q_0920.trap: (E) is on the oligohydramnios list, and the logic separates the two: fluid comes from fetal urine, so renal agenesis drains it, while anomalies that impair swallowing let it accumulate.

q_0921.topic: specific pregnancy problems and risk factors
q_0921.subtopic: too much fluid and too little
q_0921.stem: Which conditions appear on Box 26.2's oligohydramnios list?
options: Renal agenesis, prelabor rupture of membranes, prolonged pregnancy, severe growth restriction, maternal hypertensive disorders, maternal dehydration or hypovolemia, and uteroplacental insufficiency
Diabetes, twin-to-twin transfusion, and gastrointestinal obstruction
Advanced maternal age and parental chromosomal rearrangements
Autoimmune disease and multifetal gestation only
q_0921.rationale: Box 26.2 lists renal agenesis (Potter syndrome), prelabor rupture of membranes, prolonged pregnancy, severe intrauterine growth restriction, maternal hypertensive disorders, maternal dehydration or hypovolemia, and uteroplacental insufficiency.
q_0921.trap: (C) is the chromosomal abnormality list from the same box — advanced maternal age, parental chromosomal rearrangements, a previous autosomal trisomy, abnormal ultrasound findings, and an increased calculated risk from noninvasive screening.

q_0922.topic: specific pregnancy problems and risk factors
q_0922.stem: Box 26.2 splits the risk factors for intrauterine growth restriction into fetal and maternal causes. Which are the fetal causes?
options: Genetic disorders, teratogenic exposure, fetal infection, and structural abnormalities
Hypertensive disorders and pregestational diabetes
Living at a high altitude and tobacco use
Multifetal gestation and malabsorptive disease
q_0922.rationale: The fetal causes are genetic disorders, teratogenic exposure, fetal infection, and structural abnormalities. The maternal causes are hypertensive disorders, pregestational diabetes, cyanotic heart disease, autoimmune disease, restrictive pulmonary disease, multifetal gestation, malabsorptive disease or malnutrition, living at a high altitude above 10,000 feet, and tobacco or substance use.
q_0922.trap: (B), (C) and (D) are all maternal causes, and the maternal list is much the longer of the two — which is what makes a "which is fetal" item answerable by elimination if the four fetal items are held.

q_0923.topic: specific pregnancy problems and risk factors
q_0923.stem: A woman lives at 11,000 feet and smokes. Which risk does the chapter connect to these factors?
options: Polyhydramnios
Intrauterine growth restriction, since living at a high altitude above 10,000 feet and tobacco use are both maternal causes
Chromosomal abnormality
Prelabor rupture of membranes
q_0923.rationale: Box 26.2 lists "living at a high altitude (>10,000 feet)" and "tobacco/substance use/misuse" among the maternal causes of intrauterine growth restriction. Box 26.1 separately notes that smoking is associated with low-birth-weight infants, higher neonatal mortality, increased miscarriage, and increased prelabor rupture of membranes, with risks aggravated by low socioeconomic status, poor nutrition, and concurrent alcohol use.
q_0923.trap: (D) names a real smoking association from a different box, and the stem's altitude detail is what points to growth restriction specifically.

q_0924.stem: A nurse is explaining why antepartum testing is performed. Which two goals does the chapter name?
options: To identify fetuses at risk for injury from interrupted oxygenation, and to identify appropriately oxygenated fetuses so unnecessary intervention can be avoided
To determine fetal sex and estimate birth weight
To confirm the estimated date of birth and detect anomalies
To replace routine prenatal care in high-risk pregnancies
