And: "Complete emptying of the breasts through breastfeeding, hand expression, or pumping is important." The sentence that settles it: "The infection cannot be transmitted to the infant."
q_1172.trap: (A), (C), and (D) all reduce emptying of the affected breast, which is the condition that caused the mastitis in the first place — stopping makes it worse and is the most common reason breastfeeding ends prematurely.

q_1173.stem: What complications can follow untreated mastitis, and how are they prevented?
options: Breast abscess, chronic mastitis, and fungal infections of the breast; most complications can be prevented by early recognition and treatment
Permanent loss of milk production in every case
Transmission of infection to the infant
No complications occur
q_1173.rationale: Complications are "breast abscess, chronic mastitis, and fungal infections of the breast. Most complications can be prevented by early recognition and treatment."
q_1173.trap: (C) contradicts the chapter's explicit statement that the infection cannot be transmitted to the infant, and it is the belief that leads a mother to wean.

q_1174.stem: What teaching about mastitis should be given before discharge from the birth facility?
options: The signs of mastitis, and to call the health care provider promptly if the symptoms occur
Nothing, since mastitis occurs only after 6 weeks
To take prophylactic antibiotics
To wean at the first sign of breast pain
q_1174.rationale: "Breastfeeding mothers should be taught the signs of mastitis before they are discharged from the birth facility, and they need to know to call the health care provider promptly if the symptoms occur." Adequate fluid intake and a balanced diet are also important.
q_1174.trap: (D) is the action that turns a treatable infection into the end of breastfeeding, and abrupt weaning is itself on the list of predisposing factors.

q_1175.topic: classifying newborns by size and gestational age
q_1175.stem: How does the chapter define low birth weight, very low birth weight, and extremely low birth weight?
options: Less than 2500 g, less than 1500 g, and less than 1000 g respectively, with low birth weight defined regardless of gestational age
Less than 3000 g, less than 2000 g, and less than 1500 g
Less than 2500 g only for preterm infants
The categories apply only before 37 weeks
q_1175.rationale: A low-birth-weight infant is "an infant whose birth weight is less than 2500 g (5.5 lb.), regardless of gestational age"; very low birth weight is "less than 1500 g (3.3 lb.)"; extremely low birth weight is "less than 1000 g (2.2 lb.)."
q_1175.trap: (C) attaches a gestational-age condition the definition explicitly rejects, and that phrase is what allows a term growth-restricted infant and a preterm appropriately grown infant both to be low birth weight for entirely different reasons.

q_1176.topic: classifying newborns by size and gestational age
q_1176.stem: An infant's birth weight falls below the 10th percentile on intrauterine growth curves, with head circumference within normal parameters. How is this classified?
options: Small for gestational age with symmetric intrauterine growth restriction
Small for gestational age with asymmetric growth restriction, in which head circumference remains within normal parameters while birth weight falls below the 10th percentile
Appropriate for gestational age
Large for gestational age
q_1176.rationale: Small for gestational age describes "an infant whose rate of intrauterine growth was slow and whose birth weight falls below the 10th percentile." Asymmetric growth restriction is "growth restriction in which head circumference remains within normal parameters while birth weight falls below the 10th percentile," while symmetric restriction is "growth restriction in which weight, length, and head circumference all are affected."
q_1176.trap: (A) is the pattern in which everything is small, which points to a chronic, early insult rather than a late one — the same distinction Chapter 26 draws antenatally.

q_1177.topic: classifying newborns by size and gestational age
q_1177.stem: Which gestational-age boundaries does Box 34.1 give? Select all that apply.
options: Preterm is born before 37 0/7 weeks, and late preterm is 34 0/7 through 36 6/7 weeks
Early term is 37 0/7 through 38 6/7 weeks
Full term is 39 0/7 through 40 6/7 weeks
Late term is 41 0/7 through 41 6/7 weeks, and postterm is 42 0/7 weeks or more
Postterm is 41 weeks or more
q_1177.rationale: Box 34.1 gives the complete ladder: preterm before 37 0/7, late preterm 34 0/7 through 36 6/7, early term 37 0/7 through 38 6/7, full term 39 0/7 through 40 6/7, late term 41 0/7 through 41 6/7, and postterm 42 0/7 or more.
q_1177.trap: (E) moves the postterm boundary a week early, which would reclassify every late-term infant. This is the same ladder Chapter 14 gives, which is why the boundaries are worth holding once.

q_1178.topic: classifying newborns by size and gestational age
q_1178.stem: What does the chapter give as the preterm birth rate in the United States in 2021?
options: 10.48%, the highest rate since 2007, with early preterm births below 34 weeks at 2.81% and late preterm births at 7.67%
5% overall
15% overall, declining since 2007
10.48%, the lowest rate since 2007
q_1178.rationale: "The preterm birth rate in the United States in 2021 was 10.48%, the highest rate since 2007," with "the birth rate for early preterm infants (< 34 weeks gestation) was 2.81%, the highest since 2011; for LPIs (34 0/7 to 36 6/7 weeks gestation), the rate was 7.67%, the highest since 2007."
q_1178.trap: (D) inverts the trend, and the direction matters — the chapter presents these as rising, not falling.

q_1179.topic: classifying newborns by size and gestational age
q_1179.stem: Two infants both weigh 2000 g: one is preterm and one is postterm. What principle does the chapter give?
options: Their potential problems and care needs differ, and in general the closer infants are to term in gestational age and birth weight, the easier their adjustment to the external environment
Their care needs are identical because their weights are identical
The postterm infant is always sicker
Weight alone determines risk
q_1179.rationale: "The potential problems and care needs of the preterm infant weighing 2000 g (4.4 lb.) differ from those of the term or postterm infant of equal weight," and "in general, the closer infants are to term in relation to gestational age and birth weight, the easier is their adjustment to the external environment." Preterm infants "are at risk because their organ systems are immature and they lack adequate nutrient reserves."
q_1179.trap: (D) is the reasoning that would treat two 2000-g infants the same, when one has immature organs and the other has mature organs and a failing placenta behind it.

q_1180.topic: respiratory function in the preterm infant
q_1180.stem: Which structural deficits does the chapter list as putting the preterm infant at respiratory risk? Select all that apply.
options: A decreased number of functional alveoli and deficient surfactant levels
A smaller lumen in the airways with greater collapsibility or obstruction of respiratory passages
Insufficient calcification of the bony thorax and a weak or absent gag reflex
Immature and friable capillaries in the lungs, with a greater distance between functional alveoli and the capillary bed
Excessive alveolar surface area relative to body size
q_1180.rationale: The chapter lists eight deficits: decreased functional alveoli, deficient surfactant, a smaller airway lumen, greater collapsibility or obstruction, insufficient calcification of the bony thorax, a weak or absent gag reflex, immature and friable pulmonary capillaries, and a greater distance between alveoli and the capillary bed.
q_1180.trap: (E) reverses the first deficit. Fewer alveoli and a longer diffusion distance are what make gas exchange inefficient, and every later complication in the chapter traces back to this list.

q_1181.topic: respiratory function in the preterm infant
q_1181.stem: What is the normal respiratory rate for a newborn, and what are the early signs of respiratory distress?
options: 30 to 60 times per minute with significant reliance on the abdominal muscles; early signs are chest wall retractions, flaring of the nares, and expiratory grunting
12 to 20 per minute; early signs are bradypnea and apnea
60 to 80 per minute; the first sign is generalized cyanosis
30 to 60 per minute; the first sign is seesaw breathing
q_1181.rationale: "Infants normally breathe between 30 and 60 times/min, relying significantly on their abdominal muscles." Early signs of distress are "chest wall retractions, flaring of the nares, and expiratory grunting," worsening to "seesaw breathing patterns, retractions, flaring of the nares, expiratory grunting, apneic spells," with color progressing "from pink to circumoral cyanosis and then to generalized cyanosis."
q_1181.trap: (D) names a later sign as the first, which is the difference between intervening early and intervening after decompensation.

q_1182.topic: respiratory function in the preterm infant
q_1182.stem: A preterm infant has pauses in breathing lasting up to 10 seconds followed by rapid respirations. How is this classified, and how does it differ from apnea?
options: Periodic breathing, a pattern commonly seen in preterm infants; apnea is a cessation of breathing of 20 seconds or longer, or a shorter pause accompanied by bradycardia, cyanosis, or hypotonia
Apnea, requiring immediate resuscitation
Normal newborn breathing at any gestational age
Periodic breathing, which is always pathologic
q_1182.rationale: Preterm infants "exhibit up to 10-second respiratory pauses followed by compensatory rapid respirations" — periodic breathing, "a respiratory pattern commonly seen in preterm infants." Apnea is "a cessation of breathing of 20 seconds or longer, or a shorter pause accompanied by bradycardia, cyanosis, or hypotonia."
q_1182.trap: (B) treats a common pattern as an emergency, and the discriminator is not only the 20-second clock but the accompanying findings — a 12-second pause with bradycardia is apnea.

q_1183.topic: respiratory function in the preterm infant
q_1183.stem: A newborn has bluish hands and feet but a pink trunk and face. What does the Nursing Alert direct?
options: That this is acrocyanosis, a normal finding in the neonate, while central cyanosis indicates an underlying problem requiring immediate evaluation
That both findings are normal
That this requires immediate intubation
That acrocyanosis indicates cardiac disease
q_1183.rationale: The Nursing Alert states: "Acrocyanosis is a normal finding in the neonate, but central cyanosis indicates an underlying problem that requires immediate evaluation."
q_1183.trap: (B) collapses the distinction that decides whether to act. The location of the cyanosis, not its presence, is what separates a normal transitional finding from an emergency.

q_1184.topic: respiratory function in the preterm infant
q_1184.stem: Which findings suggest hypovolemia and shock in a preterm infant?
options: Hypotension, capillary refill slower than 3 seconds, continued respiratory distress despite oxygen and ventilation, and reduced urine output
Hypertension and bounding pulses
Bradycardia alone
Acrocyanosis with brisk capillary refill
q_1184.rationale: The chapter names hypovolemia and shock presenting as "hypotension, slow (>3 seconds) capillary refill, continued respiratory distress despite the provision of oxygen and ventilation, and reduced urine output."
q_1184.trap: (C) is one component of several conditions in this chapter — it appears in apnea, in cold stress, and here — and it means nothing on its own.

q_1185.topic: cold stress in the preterm infant
q_1185.stem: Which factors put the preterm infant at high risk for heat loss? Select all that apply.
options: A large surface area for body weight with minimal insulating subcutaneous fat
Limited stores of brown fat, an internal source for heat generation present in normal term infants
Fragile capillaries and decreased or absent reflex control of skin capillaries
Inadequate muscle mass activity and poor muscle tone, leaving more body surface exposed, with an immature temperature regulation center in the brain
Excessive shivering that depletes glucose stores
q_1185.rationale: The chapter lists a large surface area for body weight, minimal subcutaneous fat, limited brown fat stores, fragile capillaries, decreased or absent reflex capillary control, inadequate muscle mass activity, poor muscle tone, and an immature temperature regulation center. "Because of their large body surface in relation to their weight, preterm infants are at high risk for heat loss."
q_1185.trap: (E) attributes an adult mechanism to a newborn. Shivering appears in Box 34.2 only for "mature infants in presence of severe hypothermia" — it is a late finding, not a mechanism.

q_1186.topic: cold stress in the preterm infant
q_1186.stem: What is a neutral thermal environment, and how is it achieved?
options: The environmental temperature at which oxygen consumption is minimal but adequate to maintain body temperature, achieved with a radiant warmer bed or an incubator with control settings
The temperature at which the infant shivers least
A room temperature of 20°C
The temperature at which the infant's skin feels warm to touch
q_1186.rationale: "The goal of thermoregulation is to create a neutral thermal environment (NTE), which is the environmental temperature at which oxygen consumption is minimal but adequate to maintain body temperature," achieved with "a radiant warmer bed or ... an incubator with control settings." The nurse works against four mechanisms of heat transfer: convection, conduction, radiation, and evaporation.
q_1186.trap: (D) substitutes a subjective check for a physiologic definition, and the definition is what explains why the goal is oxygen consumption rather than comfort.

q_1187.topic: cold stress in the preterm infant
q_1187.subtopic: the cold-stress cycle and its signs
q_1187.stem: How does the chapter describe the cold-stress cycle in a preterm infant?
options: The infant tries to conserve heat and burns more calories, causing metabolism to increase and further stressing the already compromised neonate, and preterm infants have few reserves in terms of calories and fat stores
The infant shivers, generating enough heat to compensate
Metabolism decreases, conserving energy
Cold stress affects only temperature, not metabolism
q_1187.rationale: "Because preterm infants have few reserves in terms of calories and fat stores, they can easily lose heat and develop hypothermia. Cold stress results when the infant tries to conserve heat and burns more calories, causing the metabolism to increase, further stressing the already compromised neonate." The chapter calls prevention "a critical nursing role."
q_1187.trap: (C) reverses the metabolic direction, which would make cold stress an energy-sparing state rather than the energy-consuming spiral that produces hypoglycemia and acidosis.

q_1188.topic: cold stress in the preterm infant
q_1188.subtopic: the cold-stress cycle and its signs
q_1188.stem: Which findings appear in Box 34.2 as signs of hypothermia or cold stress? Select all that apply.
options: Apnea and bradycardia
Hypoglycemia, hypoxia, and metabolic acidosis
Central cyanosis, hypotonia, lethargy, and irritability
Feeding intolerance with abdominal distention, emesis, and increased residuals
A low axillary temperature as the earliest sign
q_1188.rationale: Box 34.2 lists apnea, bradycardia, central cyanosis, coagulation defects such as pulmonary hemorrhage, hypoglycemia, hypotonia, hypoxia, feeding intolerance, increased metabolic rate, irritability, lethargy, metabolic acidosis, peripheral vasoconstriction, poor weight gain with chronic hypothermia, and shivering in mature infants with severe hypothermia.
q_1188.trap: (E) names the finding that is conspicuously absent from the box as an early sign. The infant compensates first by burning glucose and oxygen, so the metabolic consequences appear before the temperature falls.

q_1189.topic: cold stress in the preterm infant
q_1189.subtopic: the cold-stress cycle and its signs
q_1189.stem: Which mechanisms of heat transfer does the nurse work against in thermoregulating a preterm infant?
options: Convection, conduction, radiation, and evaporation
Convection and conduction only
Radiation and shivering
Evaporation only
q_1189.rationale: The chapter names all four: "convection, conduction, radiation, and evaporation."
q_1189.trap: (B) drops the two that dominate in a delivery room — evaporation from wet skin and radiation to cold surfaces — and those are the two the first minutes of care are built around.

q_1190.stem: When do retinal vessels develop, and when is the retina no longer susceptible to retinopathy of prematurity?
options: They begin to form in utero at approximately 16 weeks in response to vascular endothelial growth factor and continue until maturity at approximately 42 to 43 weeks after conception; once the retina is completely vascularized, the vessels are not susceptible to ROP
They form entirely in the first trimester
They mature at 37 weeks
The retina remains susceptible throughout childhood
q_1190.rationale: "The normal retinal vessels begin to form in utero at approximately 16 weeks in response to the release of vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF). These vessels continue to develop until they reach maturity at approximately 42 to 43 weeks after conception. Once the retina is completely vascularized, the retinal vessels are not susceptible to ROP."
q_1190.trap: (C) ends the vulnerable window at term, when it actually extends past it — which is why screening continues until vascularization is complete rather than until discharge.

q_1191.stem: What mechanism does the chapter propose for the injury in retinopathy of prematurity?
options: The mechanism is unclear; fluctuating blood oxygen levels may temporarily stop the release of factors responsible for retinal vascularization, and as retinal tissue becomes hypoxic, vascular growth factors are released, producing neovascularization with capillary hemorrhages, fibrotic scarring, and possible retinal detachment
Direct oxygen toxicity burns the retina
Bright light in the nursery damages the retina
The mechanism is fully understood and is purely genetic
q_1191.rationale: "The mechanism of injury in ROP is unclear. Fluctuating blood oxygen levels may temporarily stop the release of factors responsible for vascularization of the retina. As the retinal tissue becomes hypoxic, the release of vascular growth factors occurs, and neovascularization (development of new blood vessels) occurs in the retina and vitreous, with capillary hemorrhages, fibrotic scarring, and possible retinal detachment."
q_1191.trap: (B) is the simplified version taught for decades, and the word that matters in the real mechanism is *fluctuating* — it is the swing rather than the level alone that the nursing intervention targets.

q_1192.stem: When does ophthalmologic examination for retinopathy of prematurity begin, and how long does it continue?
options: At 31 to 32 weeks, continuing until retinal vascularization is complete
At birth, with a single examination
At discharge only
At 6 months of age
q_1192.rationale: "The infant is examined by an ophthalmologist beginning at 31 to 32 weeks with examinations continuing until retinal vascularization is complete." The entire disease process in severe cases "can take several months to evolve."
q_1192.trap: (B) treats a months-long evolving process as a one-time finding, and a normal early examination says nothing about what happens over the following weeks.

q_1193.stem: What does the chapter identify as the key to managing retinopathy of prematurity, and what treatments exist?
options: Prevention and early detection, with blood oxygen levels closely monitored and significant fluctuations avoided, oxygen and ventilator settings adjusted to keep saturations within acceptable levels; treatments are laser photocoagulation or intraocular injections of anti-VEGF medications
Treatment with corticosteroids
Immediate surgery at diagnosis in every case
No treatment is available
q_1193.rationale: "The key to the management of ROP is prevention and early detection. Blood oxygen levels in the preterm infant should be closely monitored, and significant fluctuations should be avoided. Oxygen and ventilator settings should be adjusted to keep oxygen saturations within acceptable levels." Treatments are "laser photocoagulation or intraocular injections of anti-VEGF medications, which inhibit the release of VEGF."
q_1193.trap: (D) would remove the reason for screening, and the anti-VEGF treatment mirrors the mechanism exactly — the same growth factor that builds the retina drives the damage when it surges.

q_1194.stem: What is bronchopulmonary dysplasia, and in which infants does it most commonly occur?
options: A chronic pulmonary condition occurring most commonly in preterm infants requiring mechanical ventilation
An acute infection of the lungs in term infants
A congenital malformation of the airways
A complication of postmaturity
q_1194.rationale: Bronchopulmonary dysplasia is "a chronic pulmonary condition occurring most commonly in preterm infants requiring mechanical ventilation." Its etiology is multifactorial, including "pulmonary immaturity, surfactant deficiency, lung injury and stretch, barotrauma, inflammation caused by oxygen exposure, inadequate nutrition, fluid overload, ligation of a PDA, and familial predisposition."
q_1194.trap: (D) attaches the complication to the wrong end of the gestational-age ladder. Postmature infants face meconium aspiration, not the ventilator-associated chronic lung disease of prematurity.

q_1195.stem: What signs does the chapter give for bronchopulmonary dysplasia, and what is the key to its management?
options: Tachypnea, retractions, nasal flaring, increased work of breathing, and increased distress with handling and feeding; the key is prevention of prematurity and minimizing exposure to mechanical ventilation, aided by antenatal steroids, exogenous surfactant, and use of CPAP and gentle ventilation in the birth setting
Bradypnea and apnea, treated with higher ventilator pressures
Cyanosis only, treated with long-term oxygen alone
There are no characteristic signs
q_1195.rationale: Signs are "tachypnea, retractions, nasal flaring, increased work of breathing, and increased distress with handling and feeding," and "the key to the management of BPD is prevention of prematurity and minimizing exposure to mechanical ventilation," supported by "antenatal steroids, exogenous surfactant, and use of CPAP and gentle ventilation in the birth setting."
q_1195.trap: (B) escalates the exposure that causes the injury, and the pattern here matches retinopathy of prematurity exactly: the treatment that saves the infant is also what harms the organ.

q_1196.stem: What do bronchopulmonary dysplasia and retinopathy of prematurity have in common, as the chapter presents them?
options: Both are complications of the treatments that keep the preterm infant alive — oxygen and ventilation — and for both, prevention outranks treatment
Both are infections
Both occur only in term infants
Both are congenital
q_1196.rationale: The chapter presents both as the same causal family: oxygen and ventilation rescue the lungs and produce bronchopulmonary dysplasia and retinopathy of prematurity. For each, the stated key to management is prevention — avoiding oxygen fluctuations in one and minimizing ventilation exposure in the other.
q_1196.trap: (B) misclassifies the mechanism, which matters because it would point toward antibiotics rather than toward the ventilator and oxygen settings that are the actual targets.

q_1197.subtopic: the three conditions of its etiology
q_1197.stem: Which three conditions does the chapter enumerate in the etiology of necrotizing enterocolitis?
options: Intestinal ischemia, bacterial colonization of the initially sterile gastrointestinal tract with harmful organisms, and enteral feeding — especially formula feeding
Infection, dehydration, and hypoglycemia
Prematurity, jaundice, and hypothermia
Maternal diabetes, macrosomia, and birth trauma
q_1197.rationale: The chapter enumerates intestinal ischemia — from "asphyxia/hypoxia or events that cause a redistribution of blood flow away from the GI tract (e.g., hypotension, hypovolemia, severe stress)" — bacterial colonization with organisms such as Klebsiella, Escherichia coli, and Clostridium, and enteral feeding: "the majority of infants with NEC had received some type of enteral feeding."
q_1197.trap: (C) names prematurity, which is a risk factor in Box 34.6 rather than one of the three mechanisms — and knowing the mechanisms is what makes the protective factor make sense.

q_1198.subtopic: the three conditions of its etiology
q_1198.stem: A nurse is caring for a very-low-birth-weight infant. What does the chapter identify as protective against necrotizing enterocolitis?
options: Breast milk, which seems to have a protective effect — NEC is rare among infants who are exclusively fed breast milk — and probiotics such as Bifidobacterium infantis and Lactobacillus acidophilus, which assist in establishing normal bowel flora
Early formula feeding to build gut tolerance
Withholding all enteral feeding indefinitely
Prophylactic antibiotics
q_1198.rationale: "Breast milk seems to have a protective effect against the development of NEC—it is rare among infants who are exclusively fed breast milk," and "the use of probiotics such as Bifidobacterium infantis and Lactobacillus acidophilus assist in the establishment of normal bowel flora and appear to decrease the incidence of NEC."
q_1198.trap: (D) runs against the chapter's own nursing implication to "exercise antibiotic stewardship," and the evidence box notes that human milk "inhibits bacteria such as Escherichia coli, Staphylococcus aureus, and Candida from proliferating."

q_1199.subtopic: risk factors, timing, and nursing role
q_1199.stem: Which risk factors for necrotizing enterocolitis appear in Box 34.6? Select all that apply.
options: Prematurity and asphyxia
Red blood cell transfusion and early enteral or hyperosmolar feedings
Patent ductus arteriosus and congenital heart disease
Maternal smoking or cocaine use, polycythemia, and anemia
Postmaturity
q_1199.rationale: Box 34.6 lists prematurity, asphyxia, red blood cell transfusion, early enteral or hyperosmolar feedings, patent ductus arteriosus, congenital heart disease, maternal smoking or cocaine use, polycythemia, anemia, genetic predisposition, and gastrointestinal infection.
q_1199.trap: (E) is not on the list — "approximately 95% of cases occur in preterm infants," and NEC occurs in up to 5% of all very-low-birth-weight infants, with mortality as high as 50% in extremely-low-birth-weight infants.

q_1200.subtopic: risk factors, timing, and nursing role
q_1200.stem: How does the timing of necrotizing enterocolitis differ between term and preterm infants?
options: In the term infant it usually occurs between 1 and 3 days after birth but can occur as late as 1 month; in the preterm infant it usually occurs within the first 7 days but can be delayed up to 30 days
It occurs only in the first 24 hours in both
It occurs only after 1 month in both
Timing is identical in both groups
q_1200.rationale: "The onset of NEC in the term infant usually occurs between 1 and 3 days after birth but can occur as late as 1 month. In the preterm infant, NEC usually occurs within the first 7 days but can be delayed for up to 30 days."
q_1200.trap: (D) collapses two different windows, and the long tails on both mean a stable infant weeks into the stay is still at risk — which matters because "the signs of NEC are nonspecific, which is characteristic of many neonatal diseases."

q_1201.subtopic: risk factors, timing, and nursing role
q_1201.stem: Which nursing implications does the Evidence-Based Practice box give for reducing necrotizing enterocolitis? Select all that apply.
options: Exercise antibiotic stewardship
Prioritize feedings by the mother, and encourage mothers of at-risk preterm infants to provide breast milk, assisting with milk expression using an appropriate pump and meticulous hygiene
Perform meticulous hand hygiene and teach families those practices, and advocate for cleanliness in hospital cleaning practices
Advocate for proper staffing ratios, since nurse staffing is a component of the level of quality care very-low-birth-weight infants receive
Begin formula feeding early to establish gut flora
q_1201.rationale: The box's nursing implications are antibiotic stewardship, prioritizing the mother's milk, meticulous hand hygiene with family teaching, advocating for cleanliness in hospital cleaning practices, assisting with milk expression, and advocating for proper staffing ratios.
q_1201.trap: (E) reverses the feeding recommendation. Enteral feeding — especially formula feeding — is one of the three conditions in the etiology, and the mother's milk is the protective alternative.

q_1202.stem: A mother of a critically ill preterm infant grieves in preparation for her baby's possible death while still hoping the baby survives. Which parental task is this, and when does it begin?
options: Anticipatory grief, which begins during labor and lasts until the infant dies or shows evidence of surviving
Accepting that the baby is not healthy and full term
Resuming the process of relating to the infant
Learning what is unique about this baby
q_1202.rationale: In anticipatory grief, "the parent grieves in preparation for the infant's possible death, although the parent clings to the hope that the infant will survive," and the process "begins during labor ... and lasts until the infant dies or shows evidence of surviving." Its value: "being able to anticipate the loss gives families an opportunity to plan, feel more in control of their situation, and say goodbye in a special way."
q_1202.trap: (B) is the next task, "grief and depression typify this phase, which persists until the infant is out of danger and is expected to survive" — a different emotional problem with a different endpoint.

q_1203.stem: A father in the NICU appears emotionally detached and does not engage with his infant. How might the chapter frame this?
options: As definite evidence of impaired bonding requiring immediate referral

As a possible feature of anticipatory grief, in which some individuals or family members distance or detach themselves from the experience as a way of protecting themselves from the pain of loss and grief
As disinterest in the child
As a normal male response to all infants
q_1203.rationale: The chapter notes the risk within anticipatory grief: "some individuals or family members distance or detach themselves from the experience ... as a way of protecting themselves from the pain of loss and grief." The nurse's role during anticipatory grief is "to advocate for the family so that other health care professionals realize that the family is grieving. Being fully present for these families and practicing active listening are important."
q_1203.trap: (A) applies a bonding-assessment label without the grief context, and the chapter cautions that "how a parent responds to this situation depends on many factors including religious, spiritual, and cultural beliefs."

q_1204.stem: An infant is gaining weight, feeding, and weaning from the incubator, and the parents are beginning to interact more. Which parental task does this describe?
options: Anticipatory grief
Resuming the process of relating to the infant — developing an attachment that was interrupted by the infant's critical condition at birth
Adjusting the home environment
Accepting that the baby is not healthy
q_1204.rationale: "As the baby's condition begins to improve and the baby gains weight, is able to breastfeed or bottle-feed, and is weaned from the incubator or radiant warmer, the parent can begin the process of developing an attachment ... that was interrupted by the infant's critical condition at birth."
q_1204.trap: (D) belongs earlier in the sequence and ends "until the infant is out of danger and is expected to survive," which the stem's improvements suggest has already happened.

q_1205.stem: Which tasks complete the chapter's list of five parental tasks in the NICU?
options: Learning what is unique about this baby — special needs and growth patterns, caregiving needs, and growth and development expectations — and adjusting the home environment, including limiting visitors to minimize exposure to pathogens and possibly altering the environmental temperature
Choosing a pediatrician and arranging insurance
Selecting a feeding method and a car seat
Returning to work and arranging childcare
q_1205.rationale: The fourth task is "learning what is unique about this baby," covering "special needs and growth patterns, caregiving needs, and growth and development expectations," and the fifth is adjusting the home environment: "parents are encouraged to limit the number of visitors to minimize exposure of the infant to pathogens. The environmental temperature may have to be altered."
q_1205.trap: (B) and (D) are practical logistics rather than the developmental and caregiving adjustments the chapter frames as tasks.

q_1206.stem: What principle does the chapter give as the basis for involving parents in NICU care?
options: Principles of family-centered care, with nurses instrumental in helping parents learn who their infant is, recognize behavioral cues in the infant's development, and use those cues in the care they provide
That parents should observe but not participate until discharge
That care is best delivered without parental involvement to reduce infection risk
That involvement should begin only when the infant is stable enough to go home
q_1206.rationale: "Principles of family-centered care form the basis of active involvement of parents in the care of their children," and nurses "are instrumental in helping parents learn who their infant is and to recognize behavioral cues in the infant's development and to use these cues in the care they provide."
q_1206.trap: (D) delays involvement until the tasks the chapter describes have already been missed — the relating task begins as the infant improves, not at discharge.

q_1207.stem: Why does the chapter say a nurse should be present during the parents' first visit to their infant in the NICU? Select all that apply.
options: To help them see the infant rather than focus on the equipment, with the importance and purpose of the equipment explained
To explain the characteristics normal for an infant of their baby's gestational age so that parents do not compare their child with a term, healthy infant
To encourage the parents to express their feelings about the pregnancy, labor, and birth and the experience of having a high-risk infant
To assess the parents' perceptions of the infant and begin preparing them to participate in providing care
To restrict the length of the visit to reduce infant stimulation
q_1207.rationale: The chapter gives exactly these purposes for the nurse's presence at the first visit.
q_1207.trap: (E) reverses the aim of the visit, which is to bring the parents closer rather than to limit their time — "as soon as possible, the parents should see and touch their infant so that they can begin to acknowledge the reality of the birth and the infant's true appearance and condition."

q_1208.stem: How can parents be prepared before a first NICU visit?
options: When a high-risk birth is anticipated, the family can be given a tour of the NICU or shown a video; after an unexpected preterm birth, the parents can be given a booklet, view a video, or have someone describe what they will see
No preparation is possible
Only written consent is required
Preparation is discouraged because it increases anxiety
q_1208.rationale: "The family can be given a tour of the NICU or shown a video to prepare them for the sights and activities of the unit" when a high-risk birth is anticipated, and after an unexpected preterm birth, "the parents can be given a booklet, view a video, or have someone describe what they will see."
q_1208.trap: (D) withholds the preparation that makes the first sight of the unit survivable, and the first stated purpose of the nurse's presence is to help parents see past the equipment.

q_1209.stem: What does the chapter recommend about physical contact between parents and a critically ill infant?
options: Physical contact is important to establish early bonding and attachment; if parents cannot hold the infant, they can touch and stroke the baby as they speak softly, and as the condition improves they can hold the neonate and provide kangaroo care, gradually participating in feeding, bathing, and changing
Contact should be avoided until the infant is extubated
Only the mother should touch the infant
Contact should be limited to once daily
q_1209.rationale: "Physical contact with the infant is important to establish early bonding and attachment. If it is not possible for parents to hold the infant, they can touch and stroke the baby as they speak softly. As the infant's condition improves, parents can hold the neonate and provide kangaroo care. They gradually begin to participate in infant caregiving activities such as feeding, bathing, and changing."
q_1209.trap: (B) postpones all contact until a milestone that may be weeks away, when the chapter offers a graded alternative for every stage of the infant's condition.

q_1210.stem: Parents live several hours from the hospital and cannot visit daily. What methods does the chapter describe for keeping them connected?
options: Daily phone calls, notes written as if by the infant, photographs of the infant, and camera systems in some NICUs that allow parents to view their infant remotely
Weekly summary letters only
No contact until they can visit
Contact only through the primary care provider
q_1210.rationale: When parents cannot be present, "staff members devise appropriate methods to keep them informed and to help them feel connected to the newborn. Examples are daily phone calls, notes written as if by the infant, photographs of the infant. Some NICUs have camera systems that allow parents to view their infant remotely."
q_1210.trap: (C) leaves a family to imagine the worst, and the relating task the chapter describes cannot begin without some form of contact.

q_1211.stem: How does the chapter describe the experience of grandparents and siblings of an infant in the NICU?
options: Grandparents may experience grief and sadness as they watch their own children facing the difficulties of having a preterm or high-risk infant; siblings old enough to expect a new baby can be very confused when the baby must remain in the hospital, may benefit from visiting when possible, and after discharge some are bewildered and angry at the seemingly disproportionate parental time spent on the newborn
Only the parents are affected
Siblings should never visit the NICU
Grandparents are unaffected because they are not the parents
q_1211.rationale: The chapter describes grandparents' grief as they watch their own children struggle, siblings' confusion when the expected baby does not come home, the value of NICU visits when possible, and the post-discharge reaction: "some children are bewildered and angry at the seemingly disproportionate amount of parental time spent on the newborn."
q_1211.trap: (C) forecloses a visit the chapter recommends when possible, and it is often what makes the absent baby real to an older child.

q_1212.stem: What support structures does the chapter describe for NICU parents?
options: Support groups for parents of infants in NICUs, arrangements for an experienced NICU parent to contact a new group member, and referral for psychologic or family counseling when appropriate — especially for mothers, who are likely to need help expressing their feelings
No formal support is described
Only referral to social work
Support groups only for mothers
q_1212.rationale: "Some hospitals have support groups for the parents of infants in NICUs," hospitals "may arrange to have an experienced NICU parent make contact with a new group member," and "parents, especially mothers, are likely to need help in expressing their feelings and, when appropriate, can be referred for psychologic or family counseling."
q_1212.trap: (D) excludes the partner, whom the chapter includes in the tasks and in the grief, and the peer-contact arrangement is the one most easily overlooked.

q_1213.stem: How does the chapter define a postterm pregnancy and the resulting infant, and what is dysmaturity?
options: A pregnancy prolonged beyond 42 0/7 weeks is postterm, and the infant is postterm or postmature; postmaturity can be associated with placental insufficiency, producing a fetus with a wasted appearance — dysmaturity — from loss of subcutaneous fat and muscle mass
A pregnancy beyond 40 weeks, producing an infant who is always oversized
A pregnancy beyond 41 weeks, producing an infant who is always growth restricted
Postmaturity and dysmaturity are the same word
q_1213.rationale: "A pregnancy that is prolonged beyond 42 0/7 weeks is a postterm pregnancy, and the infant who is born is called postterm or postmature. Postmaturity can be associated with placental insufficiency, resulting in a fetus that has a wasted appearance (dysmaturity) at birth because of loss of subcutaneous fat and muscle mass."
q_1213.trap: (D) merges a gestational-age category with a physical description, and they are not the same: "not all postterm infants show signs of dysmaturity."

q_1214.stem: A postterm infant is large at birth with advanced development and bone age, without a wasted appearance. How should the nurse interpret this?
options: As inconsistent with postmaturity

As expected: not all postterm infants show signs of dysmaturity; some continue to grow in utero and are large at birth, and most postmature infants are oversized but otherwise normal, with advanced development and bone age
As a sign of maternal diabetes only
As evidence of inaccurate dating
q_1214.rationale: "Not all postterm infants show signs of dysmaturity; some continue to grow in utero and are large at birth. Most postmature infants are oversized but otherwise normal, with advanced development and bone age."
q_1214.trap: (A) treats the wasted appearance as required, which would make most postmature infants unclassifiable — and it is the dysmature subset, not the oversized one, that signals placental failure.

q_1215.stem: Which physical characteristics may be seen in the postmature infant? Select all that apply.
options: Dry, cracked, desquamating, parchment-like skin at birth
Firm nails extending beyond the fingertips
Depleted subcutaneous fat layers leaving the skin loose, giving an old-person appearance, with a long and thin body
Absent vernix, and possible meconium staining of skin, nails, and cord that is golden yellow to green
Abundant lanugo and thick vernix
q_1215.rationale: The chapter lists dry, cracked, parchment-like skin; firm nails extending beyond the fingertips; depleted subcutaneous fat with an old-person appearance; a long, thin body; absent vernix; and possible meconium staining, noting that an infant may show "some, but not necessarily all" of these.
q_1215.trap: (E) describes a preterm infant. Lanugo and vernix decrease as gestation advances, so their abundance points the other direction on the ladder.

q_1216.stem: Why is the perinatal mortality rate significantly higher in the postmature fetus and neonate?
options: Because during labor and birth the increased oxygen demands of the postmature fetus are not fully met, and insufficient gas exchange in the postmature placenta increases the likelihood of intrauterine hypoxia, which can result in passage of meconium in utero and raise the risk for meconium aspiration syndrome
Because postmature infants are always growth restricted
Because postmature infants cannot regulate temperature
Because of surfactant deficiency
q_1216.rationale: "The perinatal mortality rate is significantly higher in the postmature fetus and neonate," because "during labor and birth the increased oxygen demands of the postmature fetus are not fully met." And: "Insufficient gas exchange in the postmature placenta also increases the likelihood of intrauterine hypoxia, which can result in the passage of meconium in utero, thereby increasing the risk for meconium aspiration syndrome (MAS)." Watch also for fetal distress, macrosomia, and birth injury.
q_1216.trap: (D) names the preterm infant's problem. The postmature lung is mature; the placenta supporting it is not.

q_1217.stem: Parents are concerned about their postmature newborn's dry, peeling skin. What care and teaching does the chapter describe?
options: Initial bathing with a mild soap, moisturizing the skin with a petrolatum-based ointment, and helping parents understand the reasons for the dry, peeling skin
Vigorous scrubbing to remove the peeling skin
No bathing for the first week
Application of antibiotic ointment to all peeling areas
q_1217.rationale: "Initial bathing should be done with a mild soap. It can be helpful to moisturize the skin with a petrolatum-based ointment." And: "Parents may be concerned about the appearance of the postmature infant. Nurses can help them understand reasons for the dry, peeling skin."
q_1217.trap: (B) would damage already fragile skin, and the teaching half of the answer is what turns an alarming appearance into an explainable one.

q_1218.subtopic: what the immune system is missing
q_1218.stem: Which immunoglobulin crosses the placenta, and when does it reach its nadir?
options: IgG, reaching a nadir at 3 to 4 months of age for term newborns and at 3 months for preterm infants, with virtually all of the infant's IgG endogenous by 10 to 12 months
IgA, reaching a nadir at 6 months
IgM, reaching a nadir at 1 month
All immunoglobulins cross equally
q_1218.rationale: "Immunoglobulin G (IgG) crosses the placenta to provide protection to the newborn. IgG values typically reach a nadir at 3 to 4 months of age for term newborns and at 3 months for preterm infants. By 10 to 12 months of age, virtually all of the infant's IgG is endogenous."
q_1218.trap: (D) is contradicted by the next sentence in the chapter: "IgA and IgM do not cross the placenta, and both require time to reach optimal levels after birth." That gap is what colostrum partly fills.

q_1219.subtopic: what the immune system is missing
q_1219.stem: Besides immunoglobulin deficits, what other immune limitations does the chapter name in the newborn?
options: Phagocytosis is less efficient and serum complement levels are inadequate, with complement involved in immunologic reactions that kill or lyse bacteria and enhance phagocytosis; dysmaturity from growth restriction and preterm or postterm birth further compromises the immune system
The newborn has no white blood cells
Only the spleen is immature
The newborn's immune system is fully mature at birth
q_1219.rationale: "Phagocytosis is less efficient. Serum complement levels are inadequate," with complement "involved in immunologic reactions, some of which kill or lyse bacteria and enhance phagocytosis." And: "Dysmaturity seen with intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR) and preterm and postterm birth further compromises the neonate's immune system."
q_1219.trap: (D) would make the rest of the chapter inexplicable — the specific missing pieces are what determine how infection presents and how it is prevented.

q_1220.stem: Which routes of infection acquisition does the chapter describe, and what characterizes each? Select all that apply.
options: Prenatal or congenital, with organisms placentally transferred or transmitted from infected amniotic fluid, or ascending from the vagina through the cervix into the uterus

Intrapartum, through contact with an infected birth canal, with the upper airway and gastrointestinal tract as the principal pathways for generalized infections and the conjunctiva and oral cavity as the usual sites of local infection
Postnatal, acquired during resuscitation, through foreign objects such as indwelling catheters or endotracheal tubes, or through breastfeeding

Health care–associated, transferred by the hands of parents or health care personnel or spread from contaminated equipment, with the umbilicus a receptive site for cutaneous infection leading to sepsis
Through the placenta only
q_1220.rationale: The chapter describes prenatal, intrapartum, and postnatal routes with exactly these features, and names health care–associated transfer through hands and equipment, with the umbilicus as "a receptive site for cutaneous infection leading to sepsis."
q_1220.trap: (E) reduces four routes to one, and it would miss the two — intrapartum and postnatal — that nursing care most directly affects.

q_1221.stem: What consequences does the chapter attribute to prenatally acquired infection?
options: Miscarriage, preterm birth, stillbirth, and neonatal infection at birth or in the postnatal period
Only neonatal conjunctivitis
No fetal consequences
Only postnatal infection
q_1221.rationale: Prenatal infection with organisms such as herpes simplex virus, cytomegalovirus, or rubella can cause "miscarriage, preterm birth, stillbirth, and neonatal infection at birth or in the postnatal period."
q_1221.trap: (B) names a local intrapartum infection — the conjunctiva and oral cavity are "the usual sites of local infection" from contact with an infected birth canal, a different route with a different consequence.

q_1222.stem: How does the chapter define early-onset and late-onset neonatal sepsis?
options: Early-onset is invasive bacterial infection of the blood or cerebrospinal fluid occurring within the first 72 hours of life; late-onset occurs after 72 hours and up to 30 days of life
Early-onset is within 24 hours; late-onset is after 24 hours
Early-onset is within the first week; late-onset after the first month
The two terms are interchangeable
q_1222.rationale: Early-onset sepsis is "invasive bacterial infection of the blood and/or cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) that occurs within the first 72 hours of life," and late-onset sepsis occurs "after 72 hours and up to 30 days of life."
q_1222.trap: (B) moves the boundary to the first day, which would reclassify most early-onset cases and obscure the fact that the 72-hour line separates maternally transmitted infection from postnatally acquired infection.

q_1223.stem: Which organisms are associated with early-onset versus late-onset sepsis?
options: Early-onset: group B streptococci, Escherichia coli, and coagulase-negative staphylococci; late-onset: coagulase-negative staphylococci, Klebsiella organisms, enterobacter, E. coli, or Candida species
Early-onset: Candida only; late-onset: group B streptococci
Both are caused only by group B streptococci
Organisms are identical in both
q_1223.rationale: Early-onset sepsis is associated with "group B streptococci (GBS), Escherichia coli, and coagulase-negative staphylococci," and late-onset with "coagulase-negative staphylococci, Klebsiella organisms, enterobacter, E. coli, or Candida species." Early-onset is "more often associated with maternal intrapartum transmission of invasive organisms," while late-onset "can include maternally derived infection or health care–acquired infection."
q_1223.trap: (D) collapses a distinction that determines the empiric antibiotic choice, which differs between the two.

q_1224.stem: What does the chapter identify as the most significant risk factor for late-onset sepsis, and what else contributes?
options: Prematurity is the most significant risk factor; invasive procedures performed on a newborn such as intubation, catheterization, and surgery also contribute
Maternal fever is the most significant risk factor
Male sex is the most significant risk factor
There are no identified risk factors for late-onset sepsis
q_1224.rationale: "Prematurity is the most significant risk factor for late-onset sepsis," along with "invasive procedures that are performed on a newborn (e.g., intubation, catheterization, and surgery)." Entry sites include "the umbilical stump; the skin; mucous membranes of the eye, nose, pharynx, and ear; and internal systems such as the respiratory, nervous, urinary, and GI systems."
q_1224.trap: (B) is an intrapartum risk factor for early-onset disease, and the two lists sort by whether the exposure came from the mother or from the nursery.

q_1225.stem: Which intrapartum factors appear in Table 35.2 as risk factors for neonatal sepsis? Select all that apply.
options: Prelabor rupture of membranes and rupture of membranes for more than 18 hours
Maternal group B streptococcus colonization and maternal fever
Chorioamnionitis and prolonged labor
Preterm labor and maternal urinary tract infection
Maternal age over 35
q_1225.rationale: Table 35.2's intrapartum column lists prelabor rupture of membranes, maternal GBS colonization, maternal fever, chorioamnionitis, prolonged labor, rupture of membranes over 18 hours, preterm labor, and maternal urinary tract infection.
q_1225.trap: (E) is not in the table. The maternal column names low socioeconomic status, poor prenatal care, poor nutrition, and substance abuse, and the neonatal column names multiple gestation, male sex, birth asphyxia, meconium aspiration, congenital anomalies of skin or mucous membranes, galactosemia, absence of spleen, low birth weight or preterm birth, malnourishment, prolonged hospitalization, and invasive procedures.

q_1226.stem: Why has early-onset group B streptococcal sepsis declined?
options: Because of the use of intrapartum antibiotics for mothers who tested positive for GBS, which has significantly reduced the number of infants born with this life-threatening infection
Because GBS no longer colonizes pregnant women
Because of newborn antibiotic prophylaxis at birth
Because of routine cesarean birth for colonized women
q_1226.rationale: "Due to the use of intrapartum antibiotics for mothers who tested positive for GBS, there has been a significant reduction in the number of infants born with this life-threatening infection."
q_1226.trap: (C) moves the intervention from mother to infant. The prophylaxis works because it is given in labor, before the organism is transmitted.

q_1227.stem: What does the chapter say about the signs of neonatal sepsis?
options: As a general rule, the signs of early-onset sepsis are nonspecific and nonlocalizing, differential diagnosis can be difficult because the signs resemble noninfectious problems such as anemia or hypoglycemia, and late-onset signs are also nonspecific and similar
The signs are highly specific and localize to the site of infection
Fever is always present
Signs appear only after 72 hours
q_1227.rationale: "As a general rule, the signs of early-onset sepsis are nonspecific and nonlocalizing," and "a differential diagnosis can be difficult because signs of sepsis are similar to signs of noninfectious neonatal problems such as anemia or hypoglycemia." Late-onset signs "are also nonspecific and similar to the signs of early-onset sepsis."
q_1227.trap: (C) expects an adult presentation. The chapter's general list names "temperature instability (usually hypothermia)" — the newborn is more likely to be cold than febrile.

q_1228.stem: Which findings appear in Box 35.1 as clinical signs of neonatal sepsis? Select all that apply.
options: Respiratory: apnea, tachypnea, grunting, nasal flaring, retractions, cyanosis, decreased oxygen saturation, and metabolic acidosis

Cardiovascular: decreased cardiac output, tachycardia or bradycardia, arrhythmias, hypotension, and decreased perfusion with poor peripheral pulses, delayed capillary refill, and cold, clammy, or mottled skin
Neurologic: temperature instability, hypothermia or fever, lethargy, hypotonia, jitteriness, irritability, seizures, bulging fontanels, and a high-pitched or abnormal cry
Gastrointestinal: feeding intolerance with decreased suck strength and increasing residuals, vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal distention, and hypoactive bowel sounds
Localized erythema and purulent drainage at a single site
q_1228.rationale: Box 35.1 organizes the signs by system exactly as listed, and its footnote adds the laboratory findings: "neutropenia, increased bands, hypoglycemia or hyperglycemia, metabolic acidosis, and thrombocytopenia."
q_1228.trap: (E) describes a localized infection, and the chapter's point is that systemic sepsis in a newborn does not localize — which is why a subtle change across several systems is what raises suspicion.

q_1229.stem: What does the chapter say about the leukocyte count in diagnosing neonatal sepsis?
options: It is not a reliable indicator; the total neutrophil count, immature to total neutrophil ratio, absolute neutrophil count, platelet count, procalcitonin, and C-reactive protein can be used along with maternal and infant history and clinical examination
An elevated leukocyte count confirms sepsis
A normal leukocyte count rules out sepsis
No laboratory studies are useful
q_1229.rationale: "The leukocyte count is not a reliable indicator of sepsis; however, the total neutrophil count, immature to total neutrophil ratio, absolute neutrophil count, platelet count, procalcitonin, and C-reactive protein can be used, along with maternal and infant history and infant clinical examination, to diagnose sepsis." These are "likely adjuncts for the confirmation of neonatal sepsis."
q_1229.trap: (C) is the more dangerous of the two wrong readings, because it would stop a workup in an infant whose only reliable evidence is the clinical picture. Cultures of blood, cerebrospinal fluid, and urine are obtained.

q_1230.stem: What is systemic inflammatory response syndrome as the chapter defines it for the newborn?
options: A syndrome recognized by the presence of two or more of the following: hypothermia or fever, tachypnea or hyperventilation, tachycardia, bradycardia, proven or suspected sepsis, or a high or low white blood cell count
A syndrome requiring a positive blood culture
A syndrome defined by fever alone
A syndrome seen only in preterm infants
q_1230.rationale: Neonatal sepsis "can be defined as a systemic inflammatory response syndrome that may occur secondary to infection," and SIRS is "recognized by the presence of two or more of the following signs and symptoms: hypothermia or fever, tachypnea or hyperventilation, tachycardia, bradycardia, proven or suspected sepsis, or a high or low white blood cell count."
q_1230.trap: (B) requires a confirmation that often arrives after treatment must begin, and the definition deliberately includes "proven or suspected sepsis" as one criterion among several.

q_1231.stem: What complications should the nurse continue to watch for in an infant with sepsis?
options: Septicemia, meningitis, disseminated intravascular coagulation, necrotizing enterocolitis, pneumonia, and septic shock
Only pneumonia
Only jaundice
No complications are described
q_1231.rationale: The chapter names "septicemia, meningitis, disseminated intravascular coagulation, necrotizing enterocolitis, pneumonia, and septic shock," and identifies the sequelae of septicemia as "meningitis, disseminated intravascular coagulation, and septic shock." Pneumonia "is the most common form of neonatal infection" and "one of the leading causes of perinatal death."
q_1231.trap: (B) names the most common form and drops the rest, including necrotizing enterocolitis — which links this chapter's infection content directly to Chapter 34's.

q_1232.stem: Which empiric antibiotic regimens does the chapter give for early-onset and late-onset sepsis?
options: Early-onset: ampicillin and an aminoglycoside; late-onset: vancomycin and an aminoglycoside
Early-onset: vancomycin alone; late-onset: ampicillin alone
Both: penicillin G alone
Both: a third-generation cephalosporin alone
q_1232.rationale: The chapter gives "ampicillin and an aminoglycoside" for early-onset sepsis and "vancomycin and an aminoglycoside" for late-onset. "Results of blood cultures determine the need for specific antimicrobial therapy. Duration of treatment depends on the specific organism, site of infection, and the neonate's clinical response." Acyclovir and ganciclovir are the antivirals named for neonates.
q_1232.trap: (B) swaps the two regimens, and the difference tracks the organisms: coagulase-negative staphylococci acquired in the nursery are what vancomycin covers.

q_1233.stem: Which directions does the Medication Alert give for administering antibiotics to a newborn? Select all that apply.
options: Administer the prescribed dose as soon as possible after it is prepared, to avoid loss of drug stability
If the infant's IV fluid contains electrolytes, vitamins, or other medications, check with the hospital pharmacy before adding antibiotics
The antibiotic can be deactivated or can form a precipitate when combined with other substances
A secondary line of the prescribed solution may be attached with a needleless connector at the infusion site to prevent this
Antibiotics may be added directly to any running infusion without checking
q_1233.rationale: The Medication Alert gives each of these directions.
q_1233.trap: (E) is the practice the alert exists to prevent, and the consequence is either an inactivated antibiotic or a precipitate in the line of an infant already fighting sepsis.

q_1234.stem: Why is breastfeeding or human milk feeding encouraged in an infant at risk for infection?
options: Colostrum contains IgA, which offers protection against infection in the gastrointestinal tract; human milk contains an iron-binding protein that exerts a bacteriostatic effect on E. coli, as well as macrophages and lymphocytes, and passive transfer of maternal immunity reduces vulnerability to pathogens such as respiratory syncytial virus
Because human milk is easier to digest, with no immune effect
Because breastfeeding prevents all neonatal infections
Because breast milk is sterile
q_1234.rationale: "Colostrum contains IgA, which offers protection against infection in the GI tract. Human milk contains iron-binding protein that exerts a bacteriostatic effect on E. coli. Human milk also contains macrophages and lymphocytes. The vulnerability of infants to common mucosal pathogens such as respiratory syncytial virus can be reduced by passive transfer of maternal immunity in the colostrum and breast milk."
q_1234.trap: (B) treats milk as nutrition only, and the IgA point is exactly what fills the gap left by the immunoglobulin that does not cross the placenta.

q_1235.stem: What does the chapter identify as the single most important measure in preventing the spread of infection, and what other measures accompany it?
options: Hand hygiene; along with standard precautions, careful and thorough cleaning of the environment and equipment, frequently replacing used equipment, appropriate disposal of excrement and linens, and avoiding overcrowding in nurseries
Prophylactic antibiotics for all newborns
Isolation of all newborns
Routine suctioning of secretions
q_1235.rationale: "Hand hygiene is the single most important measure in preventing the spread of infection," with the other measures as listed. Newborn care procedures intended to prevent infection include "instilling antibiotic ointment in newborns' eyes 1 to 2 hours after birth, bathing, and cord care."
q_1235.trap: (D) is specifically cautioned against: "routine suctioning is not recommended and can further compromise the infant's immune status as well as cause hypoxia and increase ICP," and secretions being suctioned "may be infected."

q_1236.stem: What does the chapter give as the vaginal and rectal colonization rate for group B streptococcus among pregnant women, and what does GBS cause?
options: 15% to 35%; it is a leading cause of perinatal infections including bacteremia, endometritis, chorioamnionitis, and urinary tract infection, and in the newborn it can cause focal or systemic disease
5%; it causes only urinary tract infections
50%; it causes only neonatal disease
Under 1%; it is rarely significant
q_1236.rationale: "Among pregnant women, the vaginal/rectal colonization rate is 15% to 35%." GBS "is a leading cause of perinatal infections including bacteremia, endometritis, chorioamnionitis, and urinary tract infection. In the newborn, it can cause focal or systemic disease. GBS commonly lives in the human GI and genitourinary tracts."
q_1236.trap: (D) would make universal screening pointless, and the colonization rate is what justifies screening every pregnancy.

q_1237.stem: A mother tested negative for GBS at 36 weeks, and her newborn develops signs of infection. How should the nurse interpret this?
options: As impossible, since the screen was negative

As possible: infants born to mothers who tested negative can develop GBS infection, and GBS can also be transmitted in the birth facility from colonized health care staff or visitors, or in the community from family members or caregivers who are colonized
As evidence of a laboratory error
As late-onset disease only
q_1237.rationale: "Infants born to mothers who tested negative for GBS can develop GBS infection. GBS can also be transmitted in the birth facility from colonized health care staff or visitors or in the community from family members or caregivers who are colonized."
q_1237.trap: (A) is the reasoning that delays evaluation of a septic-appearing infant, and the chapter states the exception directly because the screen is a good test rather than a perfect one.

q_1238.stem: Which factors increase the risk for early-onset GBS disease? Select all that apply.
options: Preterm birth and rupture of membranes more than 18 hours before birth
Intrapartum maternal fever above 38°C, and a previous infant with invasive GBS disease
Maternal GBS bacteriuria during the current pregnancy
Frequent vaginal examinations, intrauterine fetal monitoring, membrane sweeping, and intraamniotic infection
Maternal age over 35
q_1238.rationale: The chapter lists preterm birth, rupture of membranes more than 18 hours, intrapartum maternal fever above 38°C, a previous infant with invasive GBS disease, maternal GBS bacteriuria in the current pregnancy, frequent vaginal examinations, intrauterine fetal monitoring, membrane sweeping, and intraamniotic infection. It also notes "an increased risk among infants born to Black women and to women less than 20 years of age."
q_1238.trap: (E) inverts the age association the chapter names — the increased risk is among women under 20, not over 35.

q_1239.stem: How do early-onset and late-onset GBS disease differ in timing and presentation?
options: Early-onset develops during the first 7 days, most often within 12 to 24 hours after birth, usually from vertical transmission from the birth canal, presenting as systemic infection or respiratory illness that mimics severe respiratory distress with rapid development of pneumonia, shock, and less often meningitis; late-onset typically occurs at 3 to 4 weeks of age and commonly manifests as bacteremia or meningitis
Early-onset occurs at 3 to 4 weeks; late-onset within 24 hours
Both present identically as meningitis
Early-onset presents only as a skin infection
q_1239.rationale: Early-onset GBS "develops during the first 7 days, most often within 12 to 24 hours after birth" and "usually results from vertical transmission from the birth canal," presenting as "systemic infection or respiratory illness that mimics the symptoms of severe respiratory distress," with rapid development of "pneumonia, shock, and, less often, meningitis." Late-onset disease occurs "at 3 to 4 weeks of age" and manifests as "bacteremia or meningitis," sometimes with osteomyelitis and septic arthritis.
q_1239.trap: (B) reverses the two windows, and the early presentation matters clinically because it looks like respiratory distress syndrome rather than like infection.

q_1240.stem: What is the usual treatment for a newborn with suspected GBS infection, and how does it change once GBS is identified?
options: Ampicillin in combination with an aminoglycoside for suspected infection; if GBS is identified as the cause, penicillin G alone may be given, with dosage and length of treatment depending on whether bacteremia or meningitis is being treated
Vancomycin alone throughout
No antibiotics until cultures return
Penicillin G alone from the start in all cases
q_1240.rationale: "The usual treatment for newborns with suspected GBS infection is ampicillin in combination with an aminoglycoside. If GBS is identified as the cause of infection, penicillin G alone may be given," and "the dosage of ampicillin and/or penicillin G and length of treatment depend on whether bacteremia or meningitis is being treated."
q_1240.trap: (C) waits for a result that takes longer than the infant has — the mortality rate for early-onset infection is 1% to 3%, with higher rates among preterm infants, and about 20% of survivors of GBS meningitis have moderate to severe neurodevelopmental impairment.

q_1241.topic: respiratory distress in the infant of a diabetic mother
q_1241.stem: Why is the infant of a diabetic mother at increased risk for respiratory distress syndrome?
options: Fetal hyperinsulinism is thought to inhibit surfactant production, leading to a delay in the maturation of the lungs; in a fetus exposed to high maternal glucose, synthesis of surfactant can be delayed because of high fetal serum levels of insulin and glucose
Because these infants are always preterm
Because maternal insulin crosses the placenta and damages the lungs
Because of meconium aspiration
q_1241.rationale: "Fetal hyperinsulinism is thought to inhibit surfactant production, leading to a delay in the maturation of the lungs." And: "In the fetus exposed to high levels of maternal glucose, synthesis of surfactant can be delayed because of the high fetal serum levels of insulin and/or glucose."
q_1241.trap: (C) has maternal insulin crossing the placenta, which it does not — the fetus makes its own in response to maternal glucose, and that is what delays lung maturation.

q_1242.topic: respiratory distress in the infant of a diabetic mother
q_1242.stem: At what gestational age does the risk of respiratory distress syndrome in the infant of a well-controlled diabetic mother become similar to the general population's?
options: At term; however, until the infant reaches 38 weeks' gestation, there is a significant increase in the risk of RDS
At 34 weeks
At 36 weeks
The risk is never comparable
q_1242.rationale: "Among infants born to women with well-controlled diabetes who give birth at term, the risk of RDS is similar to that of the general population. However, until the infant reaches 38 weeks' gestation, there is a significant increase in the risk of RDS."
q_1242.trap: (C) sets the threshold two weeks early, and the 38-week line is what makes an elective early-term birth in a diabetic pregnancy a respiratory decision as well as a scheduling one.

q_1243.topic: respiratory distress in the infant of a diabetic mother
q_1243.stem: What does the chapter say about the current frequency of respiratory distress syndrome in infants of diabetic mothers, and when is earlier birth still indicated?
options: It is much less common than in the past because of improved protocols to manage maternal glucose levels and enhanced antepartum fetal surveillance to assess lung maturity; late preterm birth may be indicated when maternal glycemic control cannot be achieved or when antepartum fetal testing is abnormal
It is more common than in the past
It is unchanged
Early birth is never indicated
q_1243.rationale: "RDS in infants of mothers with diabetes is much less common than in the past because of improved protocols to manage maternal glucose levels and enhanced antepartum fetal surveillance techniques to assess lung maturity," and "late preterm birth may be indicated in cases where maternal glycemic control cannot be achieved or for mothers who have abnormal antepartum fetal testing."
q_1243.trap: (D) removes a real indication, and the trade-off is the point: the same 38-week threshold that argues against early birth is knowingly crossed when the intrauterine environment is worse than the risk.

q_1244.stem: What does the chapter say about tobacco use in pregnancy and its effects?
options: Tobacco remains the most used substance during pregnancy, and low birth weight is its most widely recognized effect, attributed to the vasoconstrictive effects of nicotine and to carbon monoxide crossing the placenta and causing fetal hypoxemia; other outcomes include miscarriage, preterm birth, placental abruption, and placenta previa
Tobacco use has no measurable fetal effect
Macrosomia is the most widely recognized effect
Tobacco affects only the third trimester
q_1244.rationale: Tobacco "remains the most used substance during pregnancy," and "low birth weight is the most widely recognized effect," attributed to "the vasoconstrictive effects of nicotine" and carbon monoxide crossing the placenta "which can cause fetal hypoxemia." Other outcomes are "miscarriage, preterm birth, placental abruption, and placenta previa."
q_1244.trap: (C) reverses the growth effect. Nicotine constricts vessels and reduces delivery, which makes infants smaller rather than larger.

q_1245.stem: What risks does the chapter associate with secondhand smoke exposure for the infant?
options: Ear infections, respiratory illnesses such as asthma and bronchitis, and sudden infant death syndrome, with mothers and all others advised to refrain from smoking near the infant
Only mild respiratory irritation
No risks after birth
Only risks in the first week
q_1245.rationale: Secondhand smoke "increases the risk of ear infections, respiratory illnesses such as asthma and bronchitis, and sudden infant death syndrome," and "mothers and all others should refrain from smoking near the infant."
q_1245.trap: (C) ends the exposure at birth, when the postnatal risks the chapter names are among the most modifiable in newborn teaching.

q_1246.stem: How much alcohol is required to produce fetal effects, and what determines the outcome?
options: The quantity required is unclear; effects relate to the gestational age at exposure, maternal age, the amount consumed, the pattern of consumption, and maternal alcohol metabolism, and ethanol easily crosses the placenta
A specific safe threshold has been established
Only binge drinking causes effects
Only first-trimester exposure matters
q_1246.rationale: "Ethanol easily crosses the placenta. The quantity of alcohol required to produce fetal effects is unclear," with effects relating to "the gestational age at exposure, maternal age, the amount of alcohol consumed, the pattern of consumption, and maternal alcohol metabolism."
q_1246.trap: (B) supplies a threshold the chapter says does not exist, and it is the claim that makes "just a little" sound safe.

q_1247.stem: Which criteria define fetal alcohol syndrome, and how does alcohol-related neurodevelopmental disorder differ?
options: FAS requires specific dysmorphic facial features — short palpebral fissures, thin upper lip, smooth philtrum — plus growth deficiency and CNS abnormalities; alcohol-related neurodevelopmental disorder describes children with confirmed prenatal alcohol exposure who lack the facial features or growth deficits yet have structural CNS and cognitive abnormalities
Both require the facial features
FAS requires only the facial features
The two are the same diagnosis
q_1247.rationale: Fetal alcohol syndrome is "the most severe FASD and can result in fetal death," with criteria of "specific dysmorphic facial features (short palpebral fissures, thin upper lip, smooth philtrum), growth deficiency, and CNS abnormalities." Alcohol-related neurodevelopmental disorder describes children "who lack facial features or growth deficits associated with FAS, yet have structural CNS and cognitive abnormalities."
q_1247.trap: (B) would make every affected child recognizable on sight, and the chapter's closing point about this group is the opposite: "often these problems are not detected until the child goes to school and learning problems become evident."

q_1248.stem: What does alcohol-related birth defects describe, and what is the prevalence of fetal alcohol syndrome?
options: Confirmed prenatal alcohol exposure with congenital abnormalities most often including cardiac and renal anomalies, orthopedic defects, and anomalies of the eyes and ears; FAS prevalence is about 1 infant per 1000 live births in certain areas of the United States
Only neurologic abnormalities; prevalence is 1 in 100,000
Only facial features; prevalence is 1 in 10
The term is not used
q_1248.rationale: Alcohol-related birth defects describe "confirmed PAE and congenital abnormalities that most often include cardiac and renal anomalies, orthopedic defects, and anomalies of the eyes and ears." FAS prevalence is "1 infant for every 1000 live births in certain areas of the United States." The fetal alcohol spectrum disorder umbrella includes FAS, alcohol-related neurodevelopmental disorder, alcohol-related birth defects, and neurobehavioral disorder associated with prenatal alcohol exposure.
q_1248.trap: (B) reduces a multi-organ pattern to the nervous system, which is what the neurodevelopmental category covers instead.

q_1249.subtopic: why the signs cluster as they do
q_1249.stem: Why do the most common signs of neonatal abstinence syndrome reflect central nervous system irritability, increased autonomic activity, and gastrointestinal abnormalities?
options: Because opioid receptors are located in the CNS and gastrointestinal tract
Because opioids damage the liver
Because withdrawal affects only the brain
Because the infant is hypoglycemic
q_1249.rationale: "Opioid receptors are located in the CNS and GI tract. This explains why the most common signs of NAS reflect CNS irritability, increased autonomic activity, and GI abnormalities."
q_1249.trap: (C) drops the gastrointestinal half, which is where the feeding problems that drive length of stay come from.

q_1250.subtopic: why the signs cluster as they do
q_1250.stem: In what proportion of neonates exposed in utero to opioids do signs of withdrawal develop, and what determines severity?
options: 55% to 94%; withdrawal symptoms are more severe in newborns exposed to larger amounts of drugs for longer periods, and severity is also related to the timing of maternal drug use in relation to birth
Fewer than 10%; severity is unrelated to dose
All exposed infants, with uniform severity
About 25%, determined only by the specific drug
q_1250.rationale: "Signs of withdrawal develop in 55% to 94%" of neonates exposed in utero to opioids, and "withdrawal symptoms are more severe in newborns exposed to larger amounts of drugs for longer periods of time. The severity of withdrawal is also related to the timing of maternal drug use in relation to birth."
q_1250.trap: (C) removes the variability that makes assessment necessary, and Box 35.2 adds the timing rule: "the closer to birth that a mother takes the drug, the more severe the symptoms and the greater the delay in onset."

q_1251.stem: When may signs of neonatal abstinence syndrome first appear, according to Box 35.2?
options: Signs and symptoms may not be exhibited for up to 72 hours
Always within the first hour
Always within 12 hours
Not until after discharge in every case
